title: Strong-coupling efficiency–power–precision frontier
open: Derive tight, achievable bounds on efficiency, power, and output fluctuations for finite quantum heat engines with strong system–reservoir coupling, memory effects, and explicitly counted switching work.
status: Weak-coupling and restricted-model results exist; the general operational frontier remains model-dependent.
why: Distinguishes physically achievable conversion improvements from accounting artifacts.
key_works: P. P. Potts (2024), *Quantum Thermodynamics*, arXiv:2406.19206.

title: Resource-fair quantum charging advantage
open: Demonstrate a scalable quantum-battery charging advantage after matching classical and quantum devices for charger energy, interaction strength, control complexity, preparation, and readout costs.
status: Collective-charging advantages are established in models, with preliminary experiments; a broadly convincing end-to-end advantage remains outstanding.
why: Determines whether quantum batteries offer useful energy technology rather than an advantageous comparison convention.
key_works: F. Campaioli et al. (2024), *Colloquium: Quantum batteries*, DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.96.031001.

title: Long-lived, extractable quantum energy storage
open: Preserve useful extractable work in a many-body quantum battery despite decoherence and disorder, then retrieve it through experimentally realizable operations without dissipating the claimed advantage.
status: Protected states and idealized extraction protocols provide partial solutions; storage lifetime, extraction locality, and scalability remain coupled constraints.
why: Charging speed alone is insufficient for a practical storage device.
key_works: Campaioli et al. (2024), quantum-battery review, DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.96.031001.

title: Predictive thermal conductance of real interfaces
open: Predict thermal boundary conductance from a manufacturable interface’s chemistry, roughness, contamination, bonding, and intermixing, with uncertainty bounds that transfer across fabrication processes.
status: Acoustic and diffuse-mismatch models capture limited regimes; atomistic calculations and interface-mode measurements have not produced a universal practical predictor.
why: Interface resistance limits electronics cooling, thermoelectrics, and high-power energy devices.
key_works: A. Giri and P. E. Hopkins (2020), *A Review of Experimental and Computational Advances in Thermal Boundary Conductance and Nanoscale Thermal Transport across Solid Interfaces*, DOI:10.1002/adfm.201903857.

title: Nonequilibrium hotspot transport
open: Develop experimentally validated models for nanoscale hotspots where electrons and different phonon populations are not in local thermal equilibrium, including transitions back to ordinary heat diffusion.
status: Two-temperature and mode-resolved approaches exist; their parameter transferability across real alloys and interfaces remains incomplete.
why: Prevents thermal-failure predictions from depending on an ill-defined single local temperature.
key_works: Giri et al. (2020), *Electron-phonon coupling and related transport properties of metals and intermetallic alloys from first principles*; Giri and Hopkins (2020), interface-transport review.

title: Practical thermoelectric modules beyond material figures of merit
open: Convert high laboratory thermoelectric performance into inexpensive modules that retain efficiency after contact losses, thermal cycling, diffusion, oxidation, and realistic temperature gradients are included.
status: Materials optimization has progressed for decades; material-level performance does not directly determine durable module efficiency.
why: Unlocks otherwise unusable distributed waste heat.
key_works: G. J. Snyder and E. S. Toberer (2008), *Complex thermoelectric materials*, DOI:10.1038/nmat2090.

title: Tight energy bounds for metal-mediated nitrogen fixation
open: Establish achievable minimum full-cycle energy costs for metal-mediated ammonia synthesis when metal regeneration, solvent recovery, proton delivery, separation, and side reactions are all included.
status: A 2025 analysis derives limits for specified electrodeposited-metal pathways; broader reaction networks and practical attainability remain unresolved.
why: Identifies which catalyst improvements can actually reduce system energy consumption.
key_works: V. Azumah and V. Viswanathan (2025), *Fundamental Limits of Dissociative Electrochemical Ammonia Synthesis via Electrodeposited Metals*, arXiv:2507.21121.

title: Near-minimum-work desalination with real seawater
open: Approach the thermodynamic separation-work limit at useful throughput while tolerating fouling, variable salinity, pretreatment demands, membrane replacement, and environmentally acceptable brine disposal.
status: The thermodynamic limits are known and reverse osmosis is mature; the unresolved problem is the complete real-feed system, not inventing desalination.
why: Reduces the energy penalty of expanding reliable water supplies.
key_works: M. Elimelech and W. A. Phillip (2011), *The Future of Seawater Desalination: Energy, Technology, and the Environment*, DOI:10.1126/science.1200488.

title: Bankable perovskite outdoor lifetime
open: Demonstrate perovskite modules with a **proposed 25–30-year useful lifetime**, supported by validated degradation models and outdoor evidence across hot, humid, freezing, and high-irradiance environments.
status: Efficient cells and modules exist; durability and bankability remain explicit commercialization challenges in DOE’s assessment.
why: Converts attractive initial efficiency into dependable lifetime electricity.
key_works: U.S. DOE, *Perovskite Solar Cells*; M. V. Khenkin et al. (2020), stability consensus, DOI:10.1038/s41560-019-0529-5.

title: Accelerated-test-to-field transfer for perovskites
open: Establish which combinations of laboratory light, heat, humidity, electrical bias, and cycling predict outdoor degradation mechanisms and lifetime distributions.
status: ISOS-based reporting protocols were consolidated in 2020; standardized tests do not by themselves establish reliable field-lifetime extrapolation.
why: Makes warranties and technology comparisons scientifically defensible.
key_works: Khenkin et al. (2020), *Consensus statement for stability assessment and reporting for perovskite photovoltaics based on ISOS procedures*, DOI:10.1038/s41560-019-0529-5.

title: Defect-tolerant large-area perovskite manufacturing
open: Manufacture large-area films with consistently low shunt density, controlled crystallization, uniform composition, and high production yield without laboratory-only processing steps.
status: Scaling has advanced beyond small cells, but efficiency retention, reproducibility, and manufacturing integration remain distinct challenges.
why: Small-area champion cells cannot establish economical factory output.
key_works: DOE, *Perovskite Solar Cells*; J. Han et al. (2025), *Perovskite solar cells*, DOI:10.1038/s43586-024-00373-9.

title: Suppression of operational halide segregation
open: Prevent illumination- and bias-driven compositional segregation in mixed-halide absorbers while retaining the bandgap, transport, and processing properties required by tandem cells.
status: Compositional and interfacial strategies mitigate segregation in selected devices; robust suppression across operating conditions remains a materials-design problem.
why: Stabilizes voltage and spectral matching in wide-bandgap tandem absorbers.
key_works: Han et al. (2025), perovskite methods primer, DOI:10.1038/s43586-024-00373-9.

title: Stable, efficient lead-free tin perovskites
open: Control tin oxidation, self-doping, defect formation, and interface chemistry sufficiently to obtain efficient, reproducible, long-lived lead-free modules.
status: Lead-free devices exist; achieving efficiency, stability, and scalable processing simultaneously remains unresolved.
why: Offers an alternative route around lead-management requirements.
key_works: Han et al. (2025), DOI:10.1038/s43586-024-00373-9; P. K. Nayak et al. (2019), *Photovoltaic solar cell technologies: analysing the state of the art*, DOI:10.1038/s41578-019-0097-0.

title: Fail-safe lead containment
open: Retain or recover perovskite-module lead after hail, fire, flooding, prolonged weathering, and end-of-life handling without unacceptable cost or optical penalties.
status: On-device sequestration was experimentally demonstrated in 2020; comprehensive lifecycle containment is a broader requirement.
why: Addresses environmental consequences of rare but consequential module damage.
key_works: X. Li et al. (2020), *On-device lead sequestration for perovskite solar cells*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2001-x.

title: Tandem energy yield under mismatch and degradation
open: Optimize tandem architecture for lifetime energy yield under changing spectra, temperature, partial shading, and unequal subcell degradation rather than standard-test efficiency alone.
status: Tandem conversion is demonstrated; operational mismatch and reliability require architecture-specific solutions.
why: Determines whether higher cell efficiency produces more valuable lifetime energy.
key_works: Nayak et al. (2019), photovoltaic-technology analysis, DOI:10.1038/s41578-019-0097-0; DOE, perovskite commercialization assessment.

title: Kesterite photovoltage deficit
open: Identify and suppress the dominant bulk and interfacial recombination mechanisms responsible for kesterite voltage deficits without sacrificing carrier collection or manufacturing tolerance.
status: The problem has persisted through successive efficiency improvements; a 2025 study further resolves bulk recombination contributions rather than closing the deficit.
why: Could enable efficient photovoltaics using comparatively abundant constituents.
key_works: H. Ma et al. (2025), *Bulk Carrier Recombination Mechanisms and Photovoltage Deficit in Kesterite Solar Cells*, DOI:10.1002/aenm.202405033.

title: Organic photovoltaic morphology stability
open: Preserve the nanoscale donor–acceptor morphology and electrode interfaces needed for high efficiency throughout long outdoor operation and scalable coating.
status: Organic photovoltaics are established experimentally; morphology evolution and operational lifetime remain coupled to formulation and processing.
why: Enables lightweight, flexible photovoltaic applications without rapid performance loss.

title: Material-sustainable multi-terawatt photovoltaics
open: Expand photovoltaic manufacturing to sustained multi-terawatt annual output without substituting one critical-material bottleneck for another, including absorber supply, contacts, glass, energy, and recycling.
status: Haegel and colleagues’ 2023 analysis identifies scale-dependent material and manufacturing constraints; the joint supply-chain problem is not solved by cell efficiency alone.
why: Determines whether photovoltaic deployment can scale without resource-driven disruption.
key_works: N. M. Haegel et al. (2023), *Photovoltaics at multi-terawatt scale: Waiting is not an option*, DOI:10.1126/science.adf6957.

title: Silver-free contacts without reliability loss
open: Replace silver-intensive photovoltaic metallization with abundant alternatives while preserving contact resistivity, adhesion, corrosion resistance, production yield, and long service life.
status: Alternative metallization routes exist; proving their combined manufacturing and lifetime performance at very large scale remains necessary.
why: Reduces a potentially important scaling constraint.
key_works: Haegel et al. (2023), multi-terawatt photovoltaic analysis, DOI:10.1126/science.adf6957.

title: Transferable agrivoltaic design rules
open: Predict which crop, climate, soil, panel geometry, and management combinations improve combined food, water, and electricity outcomes over multiple seasons.
status: Dryland field experiments reported mutual benefits in 2019; extrapolation across crops and climates remains uncertain.
why: Avoids treating isolated successful installations as universal land-use prescriptions.
key_works: G. A. Barron-Gafford et al. (2019), *Agrivoltaics provide mutual benefits across the food–energy–water nexus in drylands*, DOI:10.1038/s41893-019-0364-5.

title: Affordable containment of hot chloride salts
subfield: Concentrating solar power and high-temperature conversion
open: Maintain economically acceptable corrosion rates in flowing high-temperature chloride salts despite impurities, thermal gradients, redox changes, and repeated startup.
status: DOE’s Generation 3 program identifies salt purification and materials compatibility as enabling research tasks for higher-temperature systems.
why: Enables hotter thermal storage and more efficient power cycles.
key_works: DOE, *Generation 3 Concentrating Solar Power Systems*; J. Vidal/NREL, *Molten Chloride Thermophysical Properties, Chemical Optimization, and Purification*.

title: Durable solid-particle solar receivers
subfield: Concentrating solar power and high-temperature conversion
open: Sustain efficient particle heating while controlling attrition, dust, agglomeration, particle loss, and nonuniform residence times through repeated commercial operating cycles.
status: Solid-particle systems advanced into DOE’s integrated pilot pathway; lifetime and integrated-operation questions remain distinct from initial heat-transfer demonstrations.
why: Makes inexpensive high-temperature solids usable as both heat carriers and storage media.
key_works: C. Ho/Sandia, *Gen3 Particle Pilot Plant: Integrated High-Temperature Particle System for CSP*; DOE Gen3 program.

title: High-temperature exchanger lifetime under cycling
subfield: Concentrating solar power and high-temperature conversion
open: Build compact heat exchangers that tolerate high pressure, corrosive media, and repeated thermal gradients without creep–fatigue cracking or prohibitively expensive materials.
status: DOE’s Gen3 research explicitly targets robust exchangers and receiver materials; component qualification remains a system bottleneck.
why: A high-temperature receiver is not useful without reliable heat transfer to the power cycle.
key_works: K. Sandhage/Purdue, *Robust High-Temperature Heat Exchangers*; DOE Gen3 CSP program.

title: Near-critical turbomachinery predictability
subfield: Concentrating solar power and high-temperature conversion
open: Predict and control compressor and turbine performance near the carbon-dioxide critical region, including real-fluid effects, off-design operation, seals, and transient instability.
status: Dedicated turbomachinery and cycle research is established; near-critical property changes complicate transferable design rules.
why: Determines whether compact supercritical-CO₂ cycles achieve their promised system benefits.
key_works: T. C. Allison et al. (2017), *Turbomachinery*, in Brun, Friedman, and Dennis, *Fundamentals and Applications of Supercritical Carbon Dioxide Based Power Cycles*.

title: Fast, efficient supercritical-CO₂ startup
subfield: Concentrating solar power and high-temperature conversion
open: Develop validated control strategies for startup, shutdown, inventory adjustment, and variable heat input that preserve efficiency and component life.
status: Steady-state cycle design is considerably more developed than complete transient operation across all intended applications.
why: Solar, storage, and flexible industrial applications cannot operate only at design point.
key_works: K. Brun, P. Friedman, and R. Dennis, eds. (2017), *Fundamentals and Applications of Supercritical Carbon Dioxide Based Power Cycles*, ISBN:9780081008041.

title: Water-sparing heat rejection without severe efficiency loss
subfield: Concentrating solar power and high-temperature conversion
open: Maintain attractive annual performance for high-efficiency thermal cycles using little cooling water in hot climates, including extreme-temperature operation.
status: Dry cooling exists; its interaction with near-critical compression and seasonal conditions creates unresolved design tradeoffs.
why: Prevents high-efficiency generation from depending on scarce water.
key_works: Brun, Friedman, and Dennis (2017), supercritical-CO₂ power-cycle volume, ISBN:9780081008041.

title: High-efficiency thermophotovoltaic storage systems
subfield: Concentrating solar power and high-temperature conversion
open: Translate high thermophotovoltaic cell efficiency into competitive electricity-to-heat-to-electricity storage after charging, insulation, optics, cooling, and auxiliary consumption are counted.
status: LaPotin et al. reported 41.1% cell efficiency under specified 2022 experimental conditions; that is not a complete storage round-trip result.
why: Could provide inexpensive, modular storage using very hot thermal reservoirs.
key_works: A. LaPotin et al. (2022), *Thermophotovoltaic efficiency of 40%*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-022-04473-y.

title: Durable thermophotovoltaic emitters and reflectors
subfield: Concentrating solar power and high-temperature conversion
open: Preserve emitter spectra, sub-bandgap photon recycling, and optical alignment through prolonged high-temperature exposure, contamination, and thermal cycling.
status: High-performance cell measurements establish conversion potential but do not settle the lifetime of complete hot optical assemblies.
why: Small optical degradation can erase system-level efficiency advantages.

title: Turbulence models for giant rotor inflow
open: Predict load-relevant turbulence, shear, veer, coherent structures, and atmospheric stability across rotor scales that span substantial fractions of the boundary layer.
status: A 2026 assessment identifies continuing gaps between atmospheric observations, simulation, and turbine-load models.
why: Reduces structural uncertainty without excessive conservative material use.
key_works: B. Kosović et al. (2026), *Impact of atmospheric turbulence on performance and loads of wind turbines: knowledge gaps and research challenges*, DOI:10.5194/wes-11-509-2026.

title: Wind-farm-cluster wake interactions
open: Predict energy extraction and wake recovery for interacting wind-farm clusters under changing atmospheric stability, coastal circulations, and mesoscale weather.
status: Individual-wake modeling is comparatively advanced; reliable coupling across turbine, farm, and weather scales remains incomplete.
why: Prevents large deployment regions from being designed as independent projects.
key_works: Kosović et al. (2026), DOI:10.5194/wes-11-509-2026; P. Veers et al. (2019), *Grand challenges in the science of wind energy*, DOI:10.1126/science.aau2027.

title: Aeroelastic stability of exceptionally large blades
open: Predict and prevent coupled bending, torsion, buckling, and aerodynamic instabilities in highly flexible rotors under realistic manufacturing variability and turbulent loading.
status: Aeroelastic tools are mature for established designs; scaling and flexibility move new machines outside well-validated regimes.
why: Enables larger rotors without disproportionate mass and failure risk.
key_works: Veers et al. (2019), DOI:10.1126/science.aau2027.

title: Floating-turbine coupled dynamics
open: Optimize turbine control, platform motion, mooring loads, and wave response together while preserving fatigue life and power production across severe sea states.
status: Floating wind has demonstrations and commercial activity; broadly validated coupled design methods remain a research frontier.
why: Expands access to deep-water wind resources.
key_works: P. Veers et al. (2022), *Grand Challenges: wind energy research needs for a global energy transition*, DOI:10.5194/wes-7-2491-2022.

title: Lifetime-positive wake steering
open: Demonstrate that coordinated wake steering increases lifetime project value after additional fatigue, actuator wear, uncertainty, and neighboring-farm effects are included.
status: Energy-gain demonstrations exist; energy-only optimization does not establish long-term net benefit.
why: Converts plant-level control from a yield experiment into dependable asset management.
key_works: Veers et al. (2022), wind-research roadmap, DOI:10.5194/wes-7-2491-2022.

title: Predictive leading-edge erosion lifetime
open: Predict coating and blade erosion from local rain, hail, salt, rotor speed, material variability, and repair history, then validate protective strategies over operating lifetimes.
status: Erosion is a recognized maintenance problem; accelerated tests and field conditions do not map through a universal lifetime law.
why: Protects aerodynamic performance and reduces expensive blade intervention.
key_works: Veers et al. (2019), wind-science challenges, DOI:10.1126/science.aau2027.

title: Floating-wind dynamic cable lifetime
open: Establish validated fatigue and failure models for power cables exposed simultaneously to platform motion, currents, thermal cycling, installation damage, and seabed interactions.
status: Existing cable engineering provides a foundation; floating systems introduce strongly coupled dynamic loading.
why: Cable failures can dominate downtime despite reliable turbines.

title: Wildlife protection with measured population benefit
open: Design siting, detection, deterrence, and curtailment policies that demonstrably reduce population-level impacts on birds and bats while quantifying displaced generation.
status: Local mitigation measures exist; population consequences and transferability remain uncertain.
why: Makes ecological protection an evaluated outcome rather than a procedural checkbox.
key_works: T. E. Katzner et al. (2019), *Wind energy: An ecological challenge*, DOI:10.1126/science.aaz9989; Veers et al. (2022).

title: Reliable small-wind performance in complex terrain
open: Predict energy yield, noise, and fatigue for small turbines in built environments and complex terrain without relying on inappropriate large-turbine or open-terrain assumptions.
status: Small-wind products exist, but highly heterogeneous inflow makes site-specific performance difficult to certify.
why: Separates genuinely useful distributed wind from poorly performing installations.
key_works: Kosović et al. (2026), atmospheric-turbulence assessment, DOI:10.5194/wes-11-509-2026.

title: Cross-fleet failure-learning datasets
open: Create interoperable, privacy-preserving wind-fleet datasets linking operating conditions, maintenance actions, component failures, and censoring so prognostic models can be tested across owners.
status: Digitalization is extensive, but fragmented formats and restricted access obstruct transferable learning.
why: Avoids repeatedly learning the same failure mechanisms within isolated fleets.
key_works: A. Clifton et al. (2023), *Grand challenges in the digitalisation of wind energy*, DOI:10.5194/wes-8-947-2023.

title: Sediment-continuous hydropower
open: Route sediment through or around reservoirs while maintaining useful storage, turbine availability, downstream geomorphology, and economically manageable maintenance.
status: Bypassing, flushing, and operational techniques have successful examples; solutions remain strongly site-dependent.
why: Addresses reservoir capacity loss and downstream sediment starvation together.
key_works: G. M. Kondolf et al. (2014), *Sustainable sediment management in reservoirs and regulated rivers: Experiences from five continents*, DOI:10.1002/2013EF000184.

title: Fish-safe turbines across species and operating points
open: Reduce injury and mortality across relevant species, life stages, heads, and part-load conditions while maintaining acceptable hydraulic efficiency.
status: Fish-friendly designs and testing exist; no single design resolves the full biological and hydraulic operating envelope.
why: Allows retrofits and operational flexibility with lower ecological damage.
key_works: DOE (2016), *Hydropower Vision: A New Chapter for America’s 1st Renewable Electricity Source*, OSTI:1330494.

title: Ecologically constrained hydropeaking
open: Schedule rapid hydropower changes while respecting species-specific ramping, habitat connectivity, temperature, and stranding constraints over entire river reaches.
status: Environmental-flow rules exist; linking short-timescale electricity value to validated ecosystem response remains incomplete.
why: Makes hydropower flexibility compatible with river health.
key_works: PNNL/DOE (2023), *Hydropower Vision Roadmap*.

title: Reservoir greenhouse-gas attribution
open: Measure net reservoir-induced emissions relative to credible pre-impoundment and alternative-land-use counterfactuals, including ebullition, drawdown zones, and downstream degassing.
status: Global syntheses exist; measurement coverage and attribution remain heterogeneous.
why: Prevents both blanket zero-emission assumptions and indiscriminate attribution of natural emissions to dams.
key_works: B. R. Deemer et al. (2016), *Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Reservoir Water Surfaces: A New Global Synthesis*, DOI:10.1093/biosci/biw117.

title: Climate-adaptive reservoir-cascade operation
open: Operate interconnected reservoirs under nonstationary inflows while jointly managing power, floods, droughts, irrigation, ecosystems, and uncertain forecasts.
status: Optimization methods are established; robust performance under changing hydrology and conflicting objectives remains unresolved.
why: Protects the reliability of existing infrastructure as historical operating rules become less informative.
key_works: PNNL/DOE (2023), hydropower roadmap.

title: Wave-energy power takeoff with storm survivability
open: Combine efficient energy capture in ordinary seas with survivability, low maintenance, and affordable power-takeoff hardware during extreme events.
status: Many converter concepts have been tested; the energy-capture–survivability–cost combination remains the core engineering challenge.
why: High average resource density is irrelevant if maintenance and storm losses dominate.
key_works: A. LiVecchi et al. (2019), *Powering the Blue Economy: Exploring Opportunities for Marine Renewable Energy in Maritime Markets*.

title: Predictive wave-energy array design
open: Predict net array production and environmental changes when hydrodynamic interactions, shared infrastructure, control policies, and device failures are coupled.
status: Single-device understanding is more developed than validated commercial-array behavior.
why: Prevents multiplication of single-device output from overstating scalable production.
key_works: L. G. Hemery et al. (2024), *Beyond Single Marine Renewable Energy Devices: A Systems-Wide Effects Approach*, OES-Environmental report, Chapter 9.

title: Statistically defensible tidal-turbine collision risk
open: Estimate collision and injury probabilities for relevant animals with sufficient statistical confidence despite rare events, imperfect detection, and behavioral avoidance.
status: Probabilistic methods and monitoring have improved; observing few collisions is not equivalent to proving negligible population risk.
why: Supports evidence-based permitting without either unsupported reassurance or unlimited monitoring.
key_works: A. E. Copping et al. (2023), *A probabilistic methodology for determining collision risk of marine animals with tidal energy turbines*; Copping and Hemery (2024), DOI:10.2172/2438587.

title: Ecosystem effects of large marine-energy arrays
open: Determine how large arrays alter sediment, mixing, food webs, habitats, and animal movement, including interactions with other ocean uses.
status: The 2024 OES assessment distinguishes relatively mature single-device knowledge from larger-scale cumulative uncertainties.
why: Commercial deployment requires evidence beyond isolated devices.
key_works: L. Garavelli et al., eds. (2024), *OES-Environmental 2024 State of the Science Report*; D. J. Hasselman et al. (2023), *“Scaling up” our understanding of environmental effects…*, Science of the Total Environment 904, 166801.

title: Autonomous marine power with low service burden
open: Deliver reliable wave- or tide-powered desalination, sensing, aquaculture, or charging systems that outperform diesel or battery replacement on complete lifecycle logistics.
status: Maritime application pathways are documented; dependable autonomous operation remains application- and site-specific.
why: Remote ocean services may provide useful markets before bulk electricity becomes competitive.
key_works: LiVecchi et al. (2019), blue-economy marine-energy report.

title: Much cheaper deep hard-rock drilling
open: Achieve a **proposed tenfold reduction in cost per successfully completed deep hard-rock well**, including bit wear, lost circulation, directional control, downtime, and failed wells.
status: Oil-and-gas drilling advances are being transferred to geothermal; consistently low-cost drilling across difficult formations remains unresolved.
why: Drilling cost and risk constrain access to geographically widespread heat.
key_works: IEA (2024), *The Future of Geothermal Energy*.

title: Superhot-well materials and completion lifetime
open: Maintain casing, cement, seals, instrumentation, and joints under superhot geothermal temperatures, aggressive fluids, and repeated thermal cycling.
status: High-temperature resource concepts are established; durable, inspectable well completions remain an enabling requirement.
why: Higher resource temperature does not automatically produce a longer-lived or cheaper well.
key_works: S. Porse et al. (2022), *Geothermal Technologies Office Fiscal Years 2022–2026 Multi-Year Program Plan*; DOE (2019), *GeoVision*.

title: Induced-seismicity-aware reservoir stimulation
open: Create useful permeability while placing reliable bounds on induced-earthquake risk, including delayed events after injection changes or stops.
status: Monitoring and traffic-light systems help manage operations; predicting fault activation and maximum event size remains uncertain.
why: Safe reservoir creation is essential to widespread enhanced geothermal deployment.
key_works: IEA (2024), geothermal outlook; DOE (2019), *GeoVision*.

title: Avoiding premature thermal breakthrough
open: Design and operate stimulated reservoirs so fluid does not short-circuit through a few fractures and exhaust useful heat long before the intended project life.
status: Circulation tests provide increasingly useful evidence, but decades-long thermal performance requires validated extrapolation.
why: Initial flow rate alone is a poor measure of durable reservoir value.
key_works: Utah FORGE, circulation-test research program; IEA (2024), geothermal assessment.

title: Time-lapse imaging of effective geothermal flow paths
open: Reconstruct the fractures that actually carry heat and fluid using sparse seismic, tracer, pressure, and temperature observations, with uncertainty suitable for operational decisions.
status: Individual sensing methods work; integrated identification remains nonunique and site-dependent.
why: Makes reservoir management less dependent on hidden subsurface assumptions.
key_works: DOE, Utah FORGE research; Porse et al. (2022), geothermal program plan.

title: Economical closed-loop geothermal heat extraction
open: Demonstrate closed-loop systems whose lifetime heat extraction justifies drilling, pumping, and surface-plant costs across clearly specified geological settings.
status: Closed-loop approaches avoid some fluid-management problems but face heat-transfer and drilling constraints; resource abundance is not proof of economical extraction.
why: Could expand geothermal where natural permeability or fluid production is unsuitable.
key_works: IEA (2024), *The Future of Geothermal Energy*.

title: Predictive geothermal scaling and corrosion control
open: Forecast and suppress mineral deposition and corrosion as geothermal fluids change pressure, temperature, gas content, and chemistry through the production cycle.
status: Treatment methods exist, but chemistry-specific failures and uncertain long-term interactions continue to limit transferability.
why: Protects wells and exchangers without excessive chemical use or downtime.
key_works: DOE (2019), *GeoVision: Harnessing the Heat Beneath Our Feet*; DOE geothermal research overview.

title: Exploration-risk reduction that unlocks finance
open: Develop exploration evidence and risk-sharing structures that reduce the cost of capital for geothermal without concealing dry-hole or poor-reservoir risk.
status: Resource assessment and public risk-sharing approaches exist; financing still depends heavily on uncertain subsurface outcomes.
why: Promising resources can remain undeveloped despite technically plausible designs.
key_works: IEA (2024), geothermal outlook; Porse et al. (2022), geothermal program plan.

title: Accelerated qualification of new reactor fuels
open: Shorten fuel-qualification timelines without weakening evidence for irradiation behavior, manufacturing variability, accident performance, and uncertainty outside tested conditions.
status: Qualification pathways exist for established fuels; advanced designs require substantial new evidence rather than automatic transfer of old experience.
why: Fuel qualification can govern deployment schedules independently of reactor construction.
key_works: National Academies (2023), *Laying the Foundation for New and Advanced Nuclear Reactors in the United States*, DOI:10.17226/26630.

title: Irradiated molten-salt chemistry
open: Predict how radiation, fission products, redox conditions, impurities, and surfaces jointly change molten-salt properties and material degradation during operation.
status: Molecular-scale experiments and calculations are active research areas; validated long-duration coupled chemistry remains incomplete.
why: Salt chemistry affects safety, instrumentation, corrosion, and maintenance simultaneously.
key_works: Brookhaven National Laboratory, *Molten Salts in Extreme Environments* research program.

title: Molten-salt component compatibility
open: Qualify structural alloys, coatings, joints, pumps, and instrumentation for flowing reactor salts under combined chemical, thermal, and irradiation stresses.
status: Historical experiments and current reactor programs provide partial evidence; compatibility remains salt- and design-specific.
why: A chemically attractive salt is not a complete maintainable reactor system.
key_works: IAEA, *Status of Molten Salt Reactor Technology*.

title: High-dose structural-material lifetime
open: Predict and control swelling, embrittlement, creep, and transmutation effects at advanced-reactor damage levels while preserving manufacturability and inspectability.
status: Radiation-resistant design strategies are established; combined high-dose performance cannot be inferred from one favorable material property.
why: Determines replacement schedules and achievable operating temperatures.
key_works: S. J. Zinkle and L. L. Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Passive safety under degraded real conditions
open: Validate passive heat-removal systems when aging, fouling, noncondensable gases, manufacturing deviations, and compound external hazards depart from ideal test conditions.
status: Passive safety concepts are not new; comprehensive design-specific validation remains necessary for new reactor classes.
why: “Passive” does not eliminate the need to quantify failure modes.
key_works: DOE, *Advanced Reactor Technologies*; National Academies (2023), advanced-reactor study, DOI:10.17226/26630.

title: Disposal-ready waste forms for advanced fuels
open: Develop and qualify waste forms and disposal pathways for advanced-reactor waste streams using explicit long-term release, package-compatibility, and lifecycle criteria.
status: Established waste-management principles provide a foundation; novel salts, fuels, and operational streams create additional qualification needs.
why: Waste disposition must be designed with the reactor, not postponed until shutdown.
key_works: National Academies (2023), DOI:10.17226/26630; IAEA, molten-salt technology assessment.

title: Remotely operated microreactor assurance
open: Establish dependable remote-operation and maintenance arrangements for microreactors, including communications loss, sensor failure, staffing, and independent verification of safe states.
status: Microreactor development is active; remote deployment combines operational challenges that cannot be resolved by miniaturization alone.
why: Remote energy applications require a credible operating model, not merely a small reactor.
key_works: DOE, *Advanced Reactor Technologies*.

title: Validated coupled multiphysics for advanced reactors
open: Quantify errors in coupled neutronics, fuel behavior, thermal hydraulics, and structural models sufficiently to support decisions outside available integral experiments.
status: Mature tools exist in individual disciplines; coupling, sparse validation data, and novel operating regimes remain important uncertainty sources.
why: Prevents precise simulation output from being mistaken for well-supported prediction.
key_works: National Academies (2023), DOI:10.17226/26630; DOE advanced-reactor research program.

title: Reproducible nuclear construction learning
open: Identify and reproduce the organizational, design, supply-chain, and regulatory conditions that lower completed-project cost and schedule risk across successive reactor builds.
status: Historical datasets show heterogeneous trajectories; published disagreement concerns comparability and explanatory interpretation, not a universal learning curve.
why: Makes cost forecasts testable rather than extrapolations from selected examples.
key_works: J. R. Lovering, A. Yip, and T. Nordhaus (2016), *Historical construction costs of global nuclear power reactors*, DOI:10.1016/j.enpol.2016.01.011; J. Koomey, N. Hultman, and A. Grubler (2017), published reply.

title: Flexible nuclear heat-and-power operation
open: Coordinate electricity generation, industrial heat extraction, and thermal storage without unacceptable fuel, component-fatigue, safety, or economic penalties.
status: Nuclear load following exists; new integrated energy configurations require design-specific dynamic validation.
why: Allows firm low-carbon heat sources to serve changing electricity and industrial demand.
key_works: DOE, *Advanced Reactor Technologies*; National Academies (2023), advanced-reactor assessment.

title: Predictive burning-plasma transport
open: Predict reactor-relevant temperature, density, rotation, and energetic-particle profiles from first principles with errors small enough to guide plant design.
status: Experiments and multiscale simulations provide major partial results; the 2026 DOE roadmap retains confinement and plasma control as core challenges.
why: Reduces dependence on uncertain extrapolation from smaller or differently heated plasmas.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*, finalized June 10, 2026.

title: Reactor-grade disruption avoidance and mitigation
open: Prevent damaging tokamak disruptions, or mitigate their consequences, with validated reliability across operating scenarios, sensor faults, and unfamiliar plasma conditions.
status: Prediction and mitigation methods exist; extremely low tolerated failure rates make reactor qualification substantially harder than retrospective classification.
why: Protects plant structures and availability.
key_works: National Academies (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI:10.17226/25991.

title: Stable detached divertor operation
open: Maintain sufficiently low target heat and particle loads while preserving core confinement, impurity control, and stability under realistic transients.
status: Detachment is experimentally established; a broad, controllable reactor operating window remains unresolved.
why: Exhaust handling can limit a plant even when the plasma produces ample fusion power.
key_works: National Academies (2021), fusion-grid study, DOI:10.17226/25991; DOE fusion roadmap.

title: Fusion-neutron material qualification
open: Qualify structural and functional materials under representative fusion-neutron spectra, temperature, stress, and accumulated damage, including helium production.
status: Fission irradiation, ion beams, and modeling provide partial evidence; representative coupled exposure remains a major qualification need.
why: Determines component lifetime and credible maintenance economics.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), radiation-resistant materials review, DOI:10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Closed tritium fuel-cycle sufficiency
open: Demonstrate integrated breeding, extraction, processing, accounting, and reinjection that maintains adequate fuel inventory after losses, decay, maintenance, and reserve requirements.
status: Blanket and fuel-cycle subsystems are under development; a positive calculated breeding ratio alone does not prove plant self-sufficiency.
why: Sustained deuterium–tritium operation requires an operable fuel economy.
key_works: DOE (2026), fusion technology roadmap; National Academies (2021), DOI:10.17226/25991.

title: Reactor-compatible plasma diagnostics
open: Measure the quantities required for control and protection despite neutron exposure, restricted viewing access, contamination, component replacement, and long operating campaigns.
status: Laboratory diagnostics are powerful; a 2026 LLNL report identifies diagnostic innovation as critical to commercialization.
why: A reactor cannot rely on measurements that disappear under its own operating conditions.
key_works: LLNL (2026), *New Report Finds Diagnostic Innovation Critical for Fusion Energy Commercialization*, reporting a DOE diagnostics workshop.

title: Radiation-tolerant high-field superconducting magnets
open: Combine high field, reliable joints, quench protection, insulation lifetime, radiation tolerance, and economically maintainable cryogenic operation.
status: High-temperature superconductors enable stronger magnets; satisfying all reactor constraints remains an integrated engineering problem.
why: Magnet performance influences confinement, plant size, maintenance, and availability.
key_works: DOE (2026), fusion roadmap; Zinkle and Snead (2014), materials assessment.

title: Manufacturable optimized stellarators
open: Preserve favorable confinement, energetic-particle behavior, exhaust access, and maintainability when optimized magnetic fields are translated into coils with realistic tolerances and assembly constraints.
status: Stellarator optimization has advanced substantially; mathematical field quality is not equivalent to an economical, maintainable plant.
why: Could combine steady-state operation with reduced disruption concerns.
key_works: P. Helander (2014), *Theory of plasma confinement in non-axisymmetric magnetic fields*, DOI:10.1088/0034-4885/77/8/087001; National Academies (2021), DOI:10.17226/25991.

title: Predictive instability and mixing control in inertial fusion
open: Predict how fabrication imperfections, drive asymmetry, and hydrodynamic instability affect fuel mixing and shot-to-shot performance across target designs.
status: Ignition and burning-plasma results are established context; a 2025 review documents continuing instability and mixing challenges.
why: Robust energy production requires reproducibility, not isolated favorable shots.
key_works: Y. Zhou (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*, DOI:10.1146/annurev-fluid-022824-110008.

title: Efficient high-repetition fusion drivers
open: Build drivers that deliver the required target conditions repeatedly with adequate wall-plug efficiency, optical lifetime, cooling, availability, and maintainable cost.
status: High-gain experimental shots do not establish the repetition rate and efficiency required by a power plant.
why: Driver electricity consumption can erase fusion energy gain at the plant boundary.
key_works: R. Betti and O. A. Hurricane (2016), *Inertial-confinement fusion with lasers*, DOI:10.1038/nphys3736; DOE (2026), fusion roadmap.

title: Mass-produced fusion targets and reliable injection
open: Manufacture, inspect, transport, and inject targets at power-plant throughput while preserving the precision and condition needed for repeatable energy gain.
status: Experimental target performance is demonstrated; economical continuous target supply is a different unsolved requirement.
why: Target logistics can dominate the economics of inertial-fusion plants.
key_works: A. B. Zylstra et al. (2022), *Burning plasma achieved in inertial fusion*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-04281-w; Betti and Hurricane (2016).

title: Net-electric fusion with useful availability
open: Demonstrate positive net electricity over a representative operating campaign after auxiliaries, downtime, maintenance, fuel processing, and component replacement are included.
status: Plasma gain, target gain, and ignition are not equivalent to this plant-level milestone; it remains the integration objective of fusion roadmaps.
why: Establishes fusion as an electricity-producing system rather than an isolated physics achievement.
key_works: National Academies (2021), DOI:10.17226/25991; DOE (2026), fusion roadmap.

title: Thin-lithium and anode-free inventory retention
open: Maintain sufficiently high practical lithium-plating efficiency in full cells with little excess lithium, realistic electrolyte quantity, useful loading, and repeated cycling.
status: Lithium-metal cells are demonstrated; excess lithium and electrolyte can conceal inventory-loss mechanisms in laboratory tests.
why: Determines whether lithium-metal energy-density gains survive realistic cell design.
key_works: C. P. Grey and D. S. Hall (2020), *Prospects for lithium-ion batteries and beyond—a 2030 vision*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-19991-4.

title: Lithium penetration through solid electrolytes
open: Prevent short-circuiting through coupled electronic leakage, defects, cracks, interfaces, and local current concentration under realistic charging and manufacturing conditions.
status: Solid electrolytes do not automatically eliminate lithium penetration; interface and mechanical behavior remain central challenges.
why: Resolves a major safety and lifetime obstacle for solid-state batteries.
key_works: J. Janek and W. G. Zeier (2016), *A solid future for battery development*, DOI:10.1038/nenergy.2016.141.

title: Low-pressure solid-state contact retention
open: Maintain electrode–electrolyte contact during plating, stripping, and volume changes without impractically high external pressure or excessive inactive structure.
status: Pressure improves some interfaces but introduces competing mechanical effects; a 2025 assessment identifies stack pressure as a critical design variable.
why: Cell-level gains can disappear when pack compression hardware is included.
key_works: Q. Li et al. (2025), *The critical importance of stack pressure in batteries*, DOI:10.1038/s41560-025-01820-x.

title: Stable silicon-anode interphases
open: Prevent repeated interphase rupture and electrolyte consumption as silicon expands and contracts, while retaining high loading, low swelling, and practical electrode density.
status: Silicon-containing commercial anodes exist; much larger silicon fractions expose unresolved lifetime and mechanical tradeoffs.
why: Increases energy density without relying entirely on lithium metal.
key_works: Grey and Hall (2020), battery outlook, DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-19991-4.

title: Stable high-capacity cathode oxygen redox
open: Exploit additional cathode capacity without unacceptable oxygen loss, transition-metal migration, voltage fade, interfacial reactivity, or safety penalties.
status: High-capacity mechanisms are experimentally established; reversibility and full-cell stability remain chemistry-dependent.
why: Raises energy density without simply increasing costly metal content.
key_works: M. Titirici et al. (2024), *2024 roadmap for sustainable batteries*, DOI:10.1088/2515-7655/ad6bc0.

title: Predictive sodium storage in hard carbon
open: Resolve how defects, layers, closed pores, surface chemistry, and precursor history determine sodium-storage voltage, first-cycle loss, and rate performance.
status: Hard-carbon sodium-ion anodes are practical; transferable structure–performance prediction remains incomplete.
why: Supports reproducible low-cost anodes from diverse feedstocks.
key_works: Titirici et al. (2024), sustainable-battery roadmap, DOI:10.1088/2515-7655/ad6bc0; ORNL, *Hard carbon anode for sodium-ion batteries*.

title: Practical room-temperature magnesium full cells
open: Combine reversible magnesium metal, compatible electrolytes, and useful cathodes at room temperature without sacrificing voltage, rate, loading, or lifetime.
status: Partial electrode and electrolyte advances exist; simultaneous full-cell performance remains the difficult requirement.
why: Tests whether magnesium’s material advantages survive electrochemical-system constraints.
key_works: Titirici et al. (2024), DOI:10.1088/2515-7655/ad6bc0; T. Kawaguchi et al. (2025), amorphous-oxide magnesium-cathode study, DOI:10.1038/s43246-025-00921-0.

title: High-utilization aqueous zinc metal
open: Cycle a large useful fraction of zinc inventory while suppressing corrosion, hydrogen evolution, shape change, and short circuits under realistic full-cell conditions.
status: Many promising results use excess zinc; practical utilization changes both lifetime and economics.
why: Establishes whether low-cost aqueous zinc can deliver low-cost stored energy.
key_works: X. Yu et al. (2023), *Ten concerns of Zn metal anode for rechargeable aqueous zinc batteries*, DOI:10.1016/j.joule.2023.05.004.

title: Lean-electrolyte lithium–sulfur cells
open: Retain high sulfur utilization and long life with high loading, little electrolyte, limited lithium excess, and realistic current collectors and packaging.
status: Sulfur’s theoretical capacity is not the unresolved issue; inactive mass, electrolyte demand, and conversion kinetics limit practical energy density.
why: Prevents impressive cathode-only metrics from overstating complete-cell performance.
key_works: G. Zhou et al. (2022), *Formulating energy density for designing practical lithium–sulfur batteries*, DOI:10.1038/s41560-022-01001-0.

title: Reversible solid-state sulfur conversion
open: Maintain ionic and electronic contact through sulfur conversion and volume changes without excessive pressure, inactive conductive additives, or low areal capacity.
status: Solid-state lithium–sulfur architectures are demonstrated; practical feasibility depends on simultaneous mechanical and transport constraints.
why: Could reduce shuttle-related losses while preserving sulfur’s energy advantage.
key_works: G. Wang et al. (2025), *Assessing the practical feasibility of solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries*, DOI:10.1038/s43246-025-00918-9.

title: Safer electrolytes without hidden performance penalties
open: Reduce flammability and harmful decomposition while retaining conductivity, interfacial compatibility, low-temperature performance, manufacturability, and affordability.
status: Multiple safer electrolyte families exist; “nonflammable solvent” is not equivalent to safe, durable full-cell operation.
why: Improves safety without trading away the function that makes batteries useful.

title: Fast charging with transferable safety guarantees
open: Select charging protocols that remain safe and life-preserving across cell variability, aging, temperature, and previously unseen duty cycles.
status: Closed-loop machine-learning optimization was demonstrated in 2020; broad transfer is harder than optimization within a controlled cell population.
why: Prevents fast charging from shifting costs into premature aging or rare failures.
key_works: P. M. Attia et al. (2020), *Closed-loop optimization of fast-charging protocols for batteries with machine learning*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-1994-5.

title: Out-of-distribution battery lifetime prediction
open: Predict remaining useful life with calibrated uncertainty for new chemistries, manufacturing batches, and operating histories without requiring full-life retraining data.
status: Early-life prediction works in studied datasets; transfer beyond the training population remains a fundamental limitation.
why: Supports warranties, second-life selection, maintenance, and financing.
key_works: K. A. Severson et al. (2019), *Data-driven prediction of battery cycle life before capacity degradation*, DOI:10.1038/s41560-019-0356-8; Attia et al. (2020).

title: Pack-scale thermal-runaway containment
open: Predict and prevent propagation across realistic packs, including aged cells, damaged interconnects, vented gases, external fire, and uncertain initial failure location.
status: Cell and pack safety methods exist; heterogeneous condition and interacting propagation mechanisms complicate universal guarantees.
why: Rare cell failures should not become catastrophic system failures.
key_works: EPRI (2024), *Energy Storage Roadmap: Vision for Advancing Energy Storage Deployment*; J. Jeevarajan et al. (2024), *Safety in the Recycling of Lithium-Ion Batteries*, DOI:10.60752/102376.27006670.

title: Spatially resolved battery pressure control
open: Measure and control nonuniform internal pressure as cells age so contact loss, localized overcompression, creep, and fracture can be avoided.
status: Average stack pressure is widely used; the 2025 pressure assessment highlights more complex mechanical–electrochemical interactions.
why: Turns pressure from an empirical assembly setting into a controllable state variable.

title: Thick, low-energy-manufactured electrodes
open: Manufacture thick electrodes with low solvent and drying requirements while maintaining adhesion, uniform transport, low defect rates, and useful fast-charge performance.
status: Dry and reduced-solvent processes are advancing; manufacturability and transport must be proven together at production scale.
why: Reduces factory energy and inactive cell mass simultaneously.
key_works: Titirici et al. (2024), sustainable-battery roadmap, DOI:10.1088/2515-7655/ad6bc0.

title: Tenfold-cheaper multiday storage
open: Achieve a **proposed tenfold reduction in levelized storage cost** for a specified multiday duty cycle against a frozen reference system, counting charging losses, replacement, financing, and balance of plant.
status: DOE’s Storage Shot and subsequent assessments formalize major cost-reduction ambitions; no chemistry-independent cost breakthrough is established.
why: Makes infrequent but prolonged renewable shortfalls affordable to cover.
key_works: DOE (2024), *Achieving the Promise of Low-Cost Long Duration Energy Storage*; DOE (2025), *Charting the Path: An Energy Earthshots Initiative Report*.

title: Decades-long organic flow-battery chemistry
open: Retain usable concentration and electrochemical capacity in inexpensive organic electrolytes over long calendar life without frequent molecule replacement or energy-intensive rejuvenation.
status: Stable molecules and improved testing exist; cycle counts alone can obscure slow chemical degradation.
why: Organic abundance does not guarantee economical lifetime storage.
key_works: J. D. Sosa and M. J. Aziz (2025), *Evaluation of Highly Stable Redox-Active Materials for Aqueous Organic Redox Flow Batteries Using Static Cells*.

title: Flow-battery membranes with low crossover and resistance
open: Combine high ionic conductivity, low active-material crossover, chemical lifetime, and low cost across changing electrolyte composition and operating conditions.
status: Commercial and experimental membranes address parts of the problem; selectivity, resistance, and durability remain coupled.
why: Membrane losses and electrolyte imbalance can dominate otherwise attractive flow chemistries.
key_works: J. Winsberg et al. (2017), *Redox-Flow Batteries: From Metals to Organic Redox-Active Materials*, DOI:10.1002/anie.201604925; MIT Energy Initiative (2022), *The Future of Energy Storage*.

title: Efficient adiabatic compressed-air storage
open: Recover compression heat and reuse it effectively across realistic storage durations and part-load operation, while controlling cavern, turbomachinery, and thermal-store costs.
status: Compressed-air storage exists; competitive adiabatic operation requires integrated thermal management rather than eliminating combustion in isolation.
why: Could provide large storage capacity with comparatively inexpensive storage volume.
key_works: MIT Energy Initiative (2022), *The Future of Energy Storage*.

title: Liquid-air storage under realistic dispatch
open: Achieve attractive round-trip efficiency and lifecycle economics without depending on unusually favorable external waste-heat or cold sources.
status: Liquid-air systems and demonstrations exist; integration assumptions strongly influence reported performance.
why: Clarifies where geographically flexible cryogenic storage is genuinely competitive.
key_works: MIT Energy Initiative (2022), storage study.

title: Predictable seasonal underground heat storage
open: Store and recover useful seasonal heat while bounding losses, groundwater interactions, thermal plume migration, geochemical changes, and effects on neighboring users.
status: Borehole and aquifer storage operate in suitable settings; transferable long-term design rules remain site-dependent.
why: Separates seasonal heat demand from short-term electricity supply.
key_works: DOE (2019), *GeoVision*; DOE geothermal technology overview.

title: Stable thermochemical storage over many cycles
open: Preserve reaction capacity, heat-transfer rate, containment integrity, and recoverable energy through repeated hydration, carbonation, or other reversible storage reactions.
status: Promising reaction pairs are known; sintering, hysteresis, side reactions, and reactor integration impede durable systems.
why: Could store heat with low standby losses and greater energy density than sensible storage.
key_works: DOE (2024), low-cost long-duration storage assessment; DOE (2025), Energy Earthshots report.

title: Low-impact closed-loop pumped storage
open: Develop economical pumped-storage projects with limited ecological disturbance, acceptable water requirements, favorable geology, and construction risks that can be credibly financed.
status: Pumped storage is mature; the unresolved problem is expanding suitable projects under contemporary siting and delivery constraints.
why: Adds long-lived storage without assuming that every topographic opportunity is developable.
key_works: DOE (2016), *Hydropower Vision*; PNNL/DOE (2023), implementation roadmap.

title: Very-low-iridium durable PEM electrolysis
open: Reduce iridium use while preserving performance and lifetime at practical current density, including catalyst dissolution, support instability, and manufacturing variability.
status: Loading reductions are demonstrated; DOE targets explicitly require simultaneous activity, durability, and cost improvement.
why: Limits exposure to a scarce catalyst material during large-scale expansion.
key_works: DOE, *Technical Targets for Proton Exchange Membrane Electrolysis*; M. Hubert et al. (2024), *Hydrogen Shot: Water Electrolysis Technology Assessment*.

title: Durable electrolyzers under intermittent power
open: Predict and minimize degradation from starts, stops, low-load periods, pressure changes, and rapid cycling while maintaining economically useful flexibility.
status: Dynamic operation is possible; lifetime under realistic renewable profiles remains distinct from steady-state durability.
why: Electrolyzer flexibility is valuable only when its degradation cost is understood.
key_works: DOE PEM-electrolysis targets; Hubert et al. (2024), electrolysis assessment.

title: Safe low-load alkaline electrolysis
open: Maintain safe gas separation and efficient operation at low current and during transients without excessive purging, standby consumption, or operating restrictions.
status: Alkaline electrolysis is mature; crossover and part-load behavior constrain flexible operating envelopes.
why: Broadens compatibility with variable electricity without creating gas-purity hazards.
key_works: DOE, *Technical Targets for Liquid Alkaline Electrolysis*.

title: Durable low-cost anion-exchange electrolysis
open: Combine stable membranes and ionomers, low-cost catalysts, useful current density, and practical water-feed conditions without sacrificing lifetime.
status: Component advances are substantial; the 2024 DOE assessment identifies integrated durability as a remaining gap.
why: Could combine favorable features of alkaline and membrane-based systems.
key_works: Hubert et al. (2024), *Hydrogen Shot: Water Electrolysis Technology Assessment*, especially the anion-exchange technology assessment.

title: Solid-oxide electrolysis under thermal cycling
open: Retain low degradation during repeated temperature and load changes while suppressing delamination, electrode coarsening, contamination, and seal failure.
status: High-temperature electrolysis offers efficient conversion under suitable conditions; flexible lifetime remains a major qualification task.
why: Couples electrolysis effectively to variable electricity and available industrial heat.
key_works: DOE, *Technical Targets for High Temperature Electrolysis*.

title: Durable proton-conducting ceramic electrolysis
open: Achieve useful full-cell performance with stable proton-conducting ceramics, steam electrodes, interfaces, and seals across realistic contaminants and operating cycles.
status: The 2024 DOE assessment treats proton-conducting solid-oxide approaches as promising but less mature than established electrolyzer classes.
why: Could reduce some high-temperature electrolysis integration penalties.
key_works: Hubert et al. (2024), electrolysis technology assessment.

title: Microbial stability of underground hydrogen storage
open: Predict and control hydrogen consumption and undesirable products from subsurface microbial activity over repeated storage cycles.
status: Hydrogen storage is not new, but porous formations introduce biological and geochemical uncertainties distinct from established salt-cavern practice.
why: Uncontrolled reactions can reduce recoverable fuel and alter gas quality.
key_works: N. Heinemann et al. (2021), *Enabling large-scale hydrogen storage in porous media – the scientific challenges*, DOI:10.1039/D0EE03536J.

title: Recoverable hydrogen in heterogeneous porous reservoirs
open: Quantify working-gas recovery, cushion-gas requirements, mixing, capillary trapping, and migration under repeated injection and withdrawal.
status: Reservoir modeling and field experience provide partial evidence; site-specific heterogeneity remains difficult to characterize.
why: Storage volume is useful only if an adequate fraction can be recovered at required purity and rate.
key_works: Heinemann et al. (2021), DOI:10.1039/D0EE03536J.

title: Hydrogen-compatible infrastructure under cyclic service
open: Establish reliable lifetime criteria for pipelines, vessels, seals, compressors, and joints exposed to hydrogen under realistic pressure cycles and material histories.
status: Compatible materials and standards exist; conversion and expanded duty cycles require asset-specific evidence.
why: Production cost reductions do not automatically produce a dependable delivery network.
key_works: IEA (2025), *Global Hydrogen Review 2025*; Heinemann et al. (2021), subsurface infrastructure discussion.

title: Low-cost, low-emission delivered hydrogen
open: Deliver hydrogen at competitive cost and verified low lifecycle emissions after electricity matching, water treatment, compression, storage, transport, and losses are included.
status: Production targets and demonstrations are not equivalent to this complete delivered-product requirement.
why: Determines whether hydrogen is useful in applications with limited alternatives.
key_works: IEA (2025), hydrogen review; Hubert et al. (2024), electrolysis assessment.

title: Reproducible aqueous nitrogen reduction
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Demonstrate useful ammonia production from nitrogen in aqueous electrochemical systems with rigorous isotope controls, contamination exclusion, complete balances, and independent replication.
status: A 2019 protocol addressed widespread measurement pitfalls; analytical rigor does not itself establish a practical synthesis route.
why: Separates genuine nitrogen fixation from trace-contamination artifacts.
key_works: S. Z. Andersen et al. (2019), *A rigorous electrochemical ammonia synthesis protocol with quantitative isotope measurements*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1260-x.

title: Sustainable continuous metal-mediated ammonia synthesis
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Sustain ammonia production with closed material cycles, non-sacrificial proton supply, acceptable electricity use, and stable interfaces rather than relying on consumable laboratory reagents.
status: Continuous operation and improved proton-management approaches were reported in 2024; full-cycle sustainability and economics remain unresolved.
why: Moves metal-mediated nitrogen fixation toward an actual industrial process.
key_works: S. Li et al. (2024), *Long-term continuous ammonia electrosynthesis*; Li et al. (2024), *Towards sustainable metal-mediated ammonia electrosynthesis*.

title: Carbon-efficient carbon-dioxide electrolysis
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Convert carbon dioxide at useful rate while minimizing carbonate formation, crossover, separation work, and unrecovered carbon losses.
status: Strong-acid multicarbon electrolysis demonstrated an important route around carbonate penalties in 2021; complete energy and carbon efficiency remain joint requirements.
why: Product selectivity alone can conceal poor feedstock and energy utilization.
key_works: J. E. Huang et al. (2021), *CO2 electrolysis to multicarbon products in strong acid*, DOI:10.1126/science.abg6582.

title: Mechanistic control of multicarbon selectivity
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Predict and control carbon–carbon coupling and product distributions under practical current density, catalyst restructuring, and changing local reaction conditions.
status: Mechanistic understanding has advanced; a 2026 review still identifies unresolved links between structure, intermediates, and selective production.
why: Reduces expensive downstream separation and empirical catalyst screening.
key_works: R. Guo et al. (2026), *Mechanistic Insights for Selective CO2 Electrolysis to Multicarbon Products*, DOI:10.1002/aenm.71009.

title: Long-lived gas-diffusion electrolysis interfaces
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Keep gas, liquid, ions, and electrons correctly distributed despite salt precipitation, flooding, drying, catalyst changes, and large-area manufacturing variation.
status: High-rate operation is demonstrated; maintaining the reactive interface over commercially relevant lifetimes remains difficult.
why: A high-performing short experiment does not establish stable industrial throughput.
key_works: Huang et al. (2021), DOI:10.1126/science.abg6582; Guo et al. (2026), DOI:10.1002/aenm.71009.

title: Low-platinum fuel cells with heavy-duty lifetime
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Reduce platinum loading while maintaining catalyst activity, support stability, membrane integrity, and useful power over demanding long-duration duty cycles.
status: Low-loading components and commercial fuel cells exist; cost and lifetime must be achieved together.
why: Determines whether fuel cells can serve high-utilization applications economically.
key_works: DOE, *Technical Targets for Polymer Electrolyte Membrane Fuel Cell Components*; DOE (2024), *Fuel Cell Technologies Subprogram Overview*.

title: Durable platinum-group-metal-free oxygen reduction
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Obtain useful acidic oxygen-reduction performance from abundant catalysts while resisting peroxide-related damage, active-site loss, and electrode transport limitations.
status: High initial activity has been demonstrated in selected materials; durable practical electrodes remain the central challenge.
why: Could reduce both cost and scarce-material dependence.
key_works: DOE, PEM fuel-cell component targets and 2024 fuel-cell research overview.

title: Fuel-flexible solid-oxide cells without rapid degradation
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Operate solid-oxide cells on relevant fuels while controlling carbon deposition, sulfur poisoning, electrode evolution, and thermal-cycle damage.
status: Solid-oxide technology is established; fuel flexibility and long life remain conditional on composition and operating strategy.
why: Expands useful fuel options without imposing costly purification and replacement.
key_works: E. Weidner et al. (2025), *Fuel Cell Technology in the European Union*, JRC144322.

title: Efficient, durable fuel-cell balance of plant
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Reduce compressor, humidification, cooling, and recirculation losses while maintaining fast response and long life across ambient conditions.
status: Stack improvements do not eliminate auxiliary-system limitations; DOE’s 2024 review includes compressor and supporting-component research.
why: System efficiency and service cost can be governed by components outside the stack.
key_works: DOE (2024), *Fuel Cell Technologies Subprogram Overview*.

title: Flexible ammonia synthesis with variable hydrogen
subfield: Fuel cells, ammonia, and electrochemical fuels
open: Operate ammonia synthesis economically under variable hydrogen supply without excessive buffer storage, catalyst damage, recycle losses, or reduced product quality.
status: Conventional synthesis is mature; flexible integration with low-emission hydrogen changes the optimization problem.
why: Reduces the need to oversize hydrogen storage and production.
key_works: IEA (2025), *Global Hydrogen Review 2025*; Li et al. (2024), sustainable ammonia electrosynthesis assessment for contrasting pathways.

title: Operationally fast, globally certified AC power flow optimization
open: Solve realistically sized nonconvex AC optimal-power-flow instances with useful global optimality certificates within operational deadlines, including stressed and atypical cases.
status: Relaxations, global methods, and strong heuristics exist; performance is instance-dependent and difficult cases remain.
why: Quantifies the cost and feasibility risks hidden by local solutions.
key_works: IEEE PES Task Force et al. (2019), *The Power Grid Library for Benchmarking AC Optimal Power Flow Algorithms*, arXiv:1908.02788.

title: Exactness boundaries for power-flow relaxations
open: Characterize broad, practically checkable conditions under which convex relaxations remain exact for meshed networks with realistic limits and operating constraints.
status: Exactness is proved for restricted settings; universal exactness is not an open conjecture—it is false in general.
why: Identifies when inexpensive certificates are trustworthy.
key_works: J. Lavaei, D. Tse, and B. Zhang (2012), *Geometry of Power Flows and Optimization in Distribution Networks*, arXiv:1204.4419.

title: Certified neutral-explicit distribution-network models
open: Construct computationally efficient relaxations for unbalanced, multiconductor networks that preserve physically meaningful voltage and grounding behavior.
status: Geth’s 2022 analysis exhibits pitfalls involving zero-voltage values; the broader task is reliable formulation and certification, not rediscovering those counterexamples.
why: Prevents apparently feasible optimization solutions from violating physical network behavior.
key_works: F. Geth (2022), *Pitfalls of Zero Voltage Values in Optimal Power Flow Problems*, arXiv:2211.03969.

title: Safe asynchronous distributed dispatch
open: Guarantee feasibility and convergence for distributed nonconvex dispatch with delayed, lost, or asynchronous communications and changing network conditions.
status: Distributed algorithms exist for structured or relaxed problems; strong guarantees weaken when realistic communications and nonconvexity are combined.
why: Enables coordination without a perfectly synchronized central optimizer.
key_works: A. Y. S. Lam, B. Zhang, and D. Tse (2011), *Distributed Algorithms for Optimal Power Flow Problem*, arXiv:1109.5229.

title: Unit commitment robust to prolonged weather scarcity
open: Schedule generation, storage, reserves, and flexible demand against correlated multi-day weather uncertainty without either excessive conservatism or unacceptable shortage risk.
status: Stochastic methods are established; rare, long-duration scarcity remains difficult to represent with tractable scenario sets.
why: Average-year adequacy can conceal expensive operational failure modes.
key_works: P. Denholm et al. (2021), *The challenges of achieving a 100% renewable electricity system in the United States*, DOI:10.1016/j.joule.2021.05.011.

title: Global transient-stability certificates for inverter grids
open: Derive useful stability certificates for heterogeneous inverter-dominated networks with nonlinear controls, current limits, protection actions, and topology changes.
status: Small-signal and restricted nonlinear analyses exist; DOE’s grid-forming roadmap identifies broader stability and modeling needs.
why: Replaces fragile extrapolation from synchronous-machine assumptions.
key_works: Y. Lin et al. (2020), *Research Roadmap on Grid-Forming Inverters*, NREL/TP-5D00-73476.

title: Selective protection with limited inverter fault current
open: Detect and isolate faults reliably when converter controls limit or reshape fault current, without misoperation during legitimate fast transients.
status: Protection approaches are evolving; AEMO published a dedicated grid-forming/grid-following fault-current assessment in 2025.
why: A stable normal operating point is insufficient if faults cannot be cleared selectively.
key_works: AEMO (2025), *Grid-Forming and Grid-Following Inverter Fault Current Contribution*.

title: Multivendor inverter interoperability
open: Establish testable interoperability requirements that predict stable combined behavior without requiring every manufacturer to reveal proprietary internal controls.
status: Grid-forming specifications and interconnection requirements already exist; consistent multivendor verification remains an active implementation challenge.
why: Prevents individually compliant devices from producing unstable aggregate systems.
key_works: ESIG, *Grid-Forming Landscape: Specifications and Interconnection Requirements*; EU DSO Entity (2025), grid-forming roadmap support document.

title: Black start without synchronous generation
open: Restore realistic networks using inverter-based resources while managing energization transients, motor loads, communication loss, and uncertain remaining infrastructure.
status: Demonstrations and grid-forming strategies exist; dependable restoration across diverse network conditions remains a system-level task.
why: Deeply inverter-based systems still need a credible recovery path after widespread outages.
key_works: EirGrid and SONI (2026), *All-Island Grid Forming Strategy*; Lin et al. (2020), NREL/TP-5D00-73476.

title: Resource adequacy with correlated technology failures
open: Quantify shortage risk when weather, fuel constraints, transmission outages, storage depletion, and common-mode equipment failures are dependent rather than independent.
status: Near-100%-renewable studies provide useful methods; dependence assumptions and extreme-event representation remain consequential.
why: Prevents overconfidence from adding nominally diverse but correlated resources.
key_works: H. Holttinen et al. (2022), *System impact studies for near 100% renewable energy systems dominated by inverter based variable generation*, DOI:10.1109/TPWRS.2020.3034924.

title: Online electric-vehicle charging with hard guarantees
open: Schedule uncertain vehicle arrivals and departures while respecting feeder limits, user commitments, fairness, and battery constraints, with explicit worst-case or probabilistic guarantees.
status: Valley-filling and online algorithms exist; guarantees depend on assumptions about forecasts, flexibility, and network models.
why: Turns a growing load into dependable flexibility.
key_works: N. Chen, C. W. Tan, and T. Q. S. Quek (2012), *Optimal Charging of Electric Vehicles in Smart Grid: Characterization and Valley-Filling Algorithms*, arXiv:1208.4743.

title: Privacy-preserving distributed energy coordination
open: Coordinate distributed resources while proving what household or business information is protected and quantifying the resulting cost, feasibility, and reliability tradeoffs.
status: Distributed optimization provides a starting point; distribution alone does not establish privacy or resistance to inference.
why: Prevents useful grid coordination from requiring unrestricted behavioral surveillance.
key_works: Lam, Zhang, and Tse (2011), distributed OPF, arXiv:1109.5229; IEEE PES Task Force (2019), arXiv:1908.02788.

title: Grid-forming recovery after current saturation
open: Design converters that return predictably from current-limited fault operation to normal grid-forming behavior without loss of synchronization or damaging secondary transients.
status: Current limitation is necessary for semiconductor protection; its interaction with grid-forming dynamics remains a central control problem.
why: Fault survival requires more than avoiding immediate device destruction.
key_works: Lin et al. (2020), grid-forming inverter roadmap, NREL/TP-5D00-73476.

title: Converter-rich harmonic stability
open: Predict and suppress harmful interactions among many converters, filters, cables, and control loops across changing network impedance and operating conditions.
status: Component-level impedance methods are established; large heterogeneous systems remain difficult to model and validate.
why: Prevents damaging oscillations that conventional frequency-stability analysis can miss.
key_works: B.-M. Hodge et al. (2020), *Addressing technical challenges in 100% variable inverter-based renewable energy power systems*, DOI:10.1002/wene.376.

title: Thermal management of ultrawide-bandgap devices
open: Preserve the electrical advantages of ultrawide-bandgap semiconductors after substrate, interface, packaging, and hotspot heat-removal limits are included.
status: Materials offer promising intrinsic limits; thermal and packaging constraints can prevent devices from reaching them.
why: Enables lower-loss, higher-power conversion rather than impressive material properties alone.
key_works: J. Y. Tsao et al. (2018), *Ultrawide-Bandgap Semiconductors: Research Opportunities and Challenges*, DOI:10.1002/aelm.201600501.

title: Useful hole conduction in ultrawide-bandgap oxides
open: Obtain controllable, useful p-type or complementary carrier transport in relevant ultrawide-bandgap materials without compensating defects destroying device performance.
status: Strong n-type and unipolar device results do not settle difficult hole-transport and doping limitations.
why: Broadens available device architectures and control strategies.
