why: Helps distinguish solver failure from genuine proximity to multiple equilibria.
key_works: S. Park et al. (2021), *Uniqueness of Power Flow Solutions Using Monotonicity and Network Topology*; H. Zhang et al. (2022), *Uniqueness of Power Flow Solutions Using Graph-theoretic Notions*.

title: Enumerating stable states of lossy grids with realistic controls
open: Extend topology-based enumeration of synchronous states to networks with voltage dynamics, reactive-power limits, converter controls, and protection transitions.
status: Delabays, Jafarpour, and Bullo showed how winding partitions organize multiple states in lossy oscillator models. Their analysis also shows that dissipation can increase multistability.
why: Reveals stable but undesirable operating states missed by a single initialization.
key_works: R. Delabays, S. Jafarpour, and F. Bullo (2022), *Multistability and anomalies in oscillator models of lossy power grids*, arXiv:2202.02439; DOI:10.1038/s41467-022-32931-8.

title: Topology learning with hidden buses and correlated disturbances
open: Recover distribution-network structure when intermediate buses are unobserved and customer disturbances are correlated, nonstationary, and affected by control actions.
status: Exact latent-node recovery is established under structured radial dynamical-system assumptions. Those assumptions are stronger than what ordinary meter datasets guarantee.
why: Enables network awareness without assuming complete, accurate utility records.
key_works: S. Talukdar et al. (2018), *Topology Learning of Radial Dynamical Systems with Latent Nodes*, arXiv:1803.02793.

title: Joint phase assignment and topology identification
open: Infer both phase connectivity and network topology from incomplete, asynchronous measurements, including mislabeled meters and changing switch states.
status: Numerous topology-identification methods are surveyed in 2024, but different methods require different observability and data-quality assumptions.
why: Correct topology with incorrect phase labels can still produce unreliable operational models.
key_works: F. Dalavi, M. E. H. Golshan, and N. D. Hatziargyriou (2024), *A review on topology identification methods and applications in distribution networks*, DOI:10.1016/j.epsr.2024.110538.

title: Distinguishing topology errors from bad measurements
open: Identify whether inconsistent observations originate from an incorrect network model, faulty sensors, unmodeled injections, or several simultaneous causes.
status: Robust estimators and topology-error detectors exist. Their guarantees do not automatically survive multiple correlated errors and poorly observable regions.
why: Prevents an estimator from “correcting” good measurements to fit a wrong network.
key_works: S. Park, R. Mohammadi-Ghazi, and J. Lavaei (2021), *Nonlinear Least Absolute Value Estimator for Topology Error Detection and Robust State Estimation*, IEEE Access 9, 137198–137210.

title: Elimination or certification of spurious state-estimation minima
open: Characterize when nonlinear state estimators possess misleading local minima, and develop algorithms that either avoid them or certify that a returned estimate is globally adequate.
status: Spurious local minima have been studied explicitly. Convexity or benign behavior in a restricted formulation does not establish it for every measurement layout.
why: A numerically converged estimate can still be physically wrong.
key_works: R. Y. Zhang and J. Lavaei (2019), *Spurious Local Minima in Power System State Estimation*.

title: Braess-safe network reinforcement
open: Identify network additions or capacity upgrades that cannot worsen specified congestion or stability metrics over a defined uncertainty set, or derive conditions showing when such guarantees are impossible.
status: Braess-type worsening in power grids has been analyzed and demonstrated in models. The existence of the paradox is solved context; safe intervention selection remains open.
why: More infrastructure does not automatically improve every network outcome.
key_works: B. Schäfer et al. (2022), *Understanding Braess’ paradox in power grids*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-022-32917-6.

title: Cascading-failure prediction with actual protection dynamics
open: Predict cascade pathways when transient power swings, relay timing, hidden failures, thermal limits, and operator actions interact.
status: Dynamic models show cascade mechanisms absent from static overload analyses. Comprehensive validation against real event sequences remains difficult.
why: Determines which interventions stop a cascade rather than merely improve its initial state.
key_works: B. Schäfer et al. (2018), *Dynamically induced cascading failures in power grids*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-018-04287-5.

title: Certified transmission switching at operational scale
open: Select beneficial switching actions with explicit feasibility and optimality guarantees while accounting for nonlinear AC behavior, transient security, and uncertain conditions.
status: Stronger formulations and bounds improve optimal-transmission-switching algorithms. Combining operational speed with complete physical security remains unresolved.
why: Switching can create useful flexibility but also remove critical stability margins.
key_works: S. Fattahi, J. Lavaei, and A. Atamtürk (2018), *A Bound Strengthening Method for Optimal Transmission Switching in Power Systems*.

title: Valid chance constraints under changing tail dependence
open: Enforce probabilistic network limits when renewable output and demand have heavy tails, spatial dependence, and distributions that change after the training period.
status: Data-driven stochastic AC optimization and importance-sampling approaches exist. Their guarantees depend on distributional assumptions and sampling coverage.
why: Nominally small violation probabilities can be misleading when rare joint events are omitted.
key_works: I. Mezghani, S. Misra, and D. Deka (2020), *Stochastic AC optimal power flow: A data-driven approach*, Electric Power Systems Research 189, 106567; arXiv:2111.11729.

title: Detectability limits for coordinated grid-data manipulation
open: Characterize which coordinated measurement manipulations are fundamentally indistinguishable from legitimate system behavior under a specified sensor and trust model, then identify minimal additional safeguards.
status: Cybersecurity research establishes that attack detection depends on observability, trusted measurements, and physical assumptions. More anomaly-detection training cannot remove an information-theoretic ambiguity.
why: Directs investment toward missing evidence rather than unattainable detector accuracy.
key_works: T. Krause et al. (2021), *Cybersecurity in Power Grids: Challenges and Opportunities*, PMCID:PMC8473297.

title: Error-bounded reduced models for expanding DC grids
open: Reduce detailed converter-network models while bounding errors across the frequency range and operating changes relevant to stability studies, including later network extensions.
status: A 2025 InterOPERA study reduced a model from order 47 to order 5 and validated a specified frequency range. Such demonstrations do not provide universal error guarantees under expansion.
why: Makes large multivendor studies tractable without concealing unstable interactions.
key_works: M. Elsodany et al. (2025), *Development of Frequency-Dependent DC Equivalent Models for Multi-Terminal DC Grids*.

title: Tracking obsolete black-box converter equivalents
open: Detect when a previously validated converter equivalent becomes inaccurate because of firmware, settings, temperature, aging, or changed surrounding equipment.
status: Frequency-dependent equivalents improve on ideal DC-source representations, but they remain models of particular operating conditions and implementations.
why: A model can remain executable long after it stops representing the installed asset.
key_works: Elsodany et al. (2025), *Development of Frequency-Dependent DC Equivalent Models for Multi-Terminal DC Grids*.

title: Coupled AC-forming and DC-voltage-control stability
open: Establish operating-region guarantees when a converter simultaneously supports AC grid formation and DC-voltage regulation while facing finite stored energy and current limits.
status: InterOPERA’s 2025 three-terminal study compares grid-forming and DC-droop combinations. Small-signal compatibility of selected combinations does not establish global fault recovery.
why: Stabilizing one side of a converter can destabilize the other.
key_works: M. Elsodany et al. (2025), *Analysis of Interoperability between DC-Voltage-Droop-Controlled MMCs with Grid-Forming Functionality in an MTDC Grid*.

title: Joint DC-breaker, reactor, and control co-design
open: Optimize fault-clearing time, breaker energy absorption, limiting-reactor size, insulation stress, and post-fault control together over credible network faults.
status: DC breakers and protection architectures exist. InterOPERA’s transient study illustrates the interdependence of fault behavior and equipment sizing.
why: Optimizing each component separately can produce an expensive or poorly coordinated protection system.
key_works: B. de Foucaud et al. (2025), *Multi-Terminal Multi-Vendor HVDC Grid Design Studies—Part III: Transient Study*.

title: Pole-to-ground fault recovery in multivendor bipolar grids
open: Maintain predictable healthy-pole operation and restore the failed pole while controlling temporary overvoltages, asymmetric currents, and converter-specific blocking behavior.
status: Detailed bipolar transient studies exist. Generalizing their conclusions across grounding arrangements and vendor implementations remains a qualification problem.
why: A single-pole fault should not unnecessarily become a complete corridor outage.
key_works: de Foucaud et al. (2025), *Multi-Terminal Multi-Vendor HVDC Grid Design Studies—Part III*.

title: Cross-simulator equivalence of proprietary converter models
open: Establish reproducible tests showing that offline, software-in-the-loop, and controller-replica models produce sufficiently equivalent behavior despite different numerical solvers and interfaces.
status: InterOPERA published approximately 150 model and replica requirements in 2025. Requirements are a foundation, not proof of behavioral equivalence for every implementation.
why: Otherwise, “interoperability passed” can depend on the simulation platform.
key_works: InterOPERA (2025), Deliverable D1.1, *Requirements for AC/DC converter stations, DC switching stations, Power Park modules and DC Grid controller offline models, SIL models and C&P cubicles*.

title: Decades-long availability of executable control replicas
open: Establish technical and contractual arrangements that keep validated converter-control models and replicas usable after vendor changes, software obsolescence, and repeated upgrades.
status: InterOPERA’s requirements explicitly place long-term replica maintenance outside its project scope and identify commercial arrangements as necessary.
why: Long-lived infrastructure needs testable behavior throughout its lifetime, not only at commissioning.
key_works: InterOPERA (2025), D1.1 model and control-replica requirements.

title: Responsibility allocation for multivendor interaction failures
open: Design procurement and assurance arrangements that resolve responsibility when individually compliant components interact badly, without requiring a single vendor to own the entire network.
status: InterOPERA’s July 2026 procurement work assesses risks and alternative procurement approaches. Durable allocation of integration and update obligations remains an implementation problem.
why: Unallocated interaction risk can block otherwise technically viable interoperable networks.
key_works: InterOPERA (2026), *Risk Assessment and Procurement Strategy*.

title: Prices consistent with sequential dispatch decisions
open: Construct pricing rules whose investment and operating incentives remain appropriate when dispatch uses rolling forecasts, intertemporal constraints, and approximation algorithms.
status: Mays finds that dispatch policies with similar operating costs can produce substantially different storage revenues. Operational near-optimality does not imply economically similar prices.
why: Assets respond to prices generated by actual algorithms, not an idealized perfect-foresight solution.
key_works: J. Mays (2024), *Sequential pricing of electricity*, DOI:10.1016/j.eneco.2024.107790.

title: Efficient investment incentives under nonconvex pricing
open: Identify pricing and supplementary-payment rules that support efficient long-run investment when startup costs, minimum output, storage constraints, and indivisible capacity prevent ordinary convex-market results.
status: Convex-hull pricing and alternative approaches address parts of the problem. Different desirable properties—cost recovery, efficient dispatch, transparent prices, and investment incentives—need not coincide.
why: A market can operate existing assets reasonably while inducing the wrong future mix.
key_works: N. Azizan et al. (2020), *Optimal Pricing in Markets with Nonconvex Costs*, Operations Research 68, 480–496; J. Mays et al. (2021), *Investment effects of pricing schemes for non-convex markets*.

title: Manipulation-resistant cost-causation charges for reserves
open: Allocate reserve and contingency costs according to causal contributions while preventing strategic changes in offers, asset aggregation, or declared reliability from gaming the allocation.
status: Ribeiro et al. propose a causation-based framework with revenue-adequacy properties in 2025. Strategic behavior under richer information and uncertainty is a further question.
why: Cost-reflective charges should encourage actual reliability improvements rather than accounting changes.
key_works: L. Ribeiro et al. (2025), *A Causation-Based Framework for Pricing and Cost Allocation of Energy, Reserves, and Transmission in Modern Power Systems*, arXiv:2505.24159.

title: Stable reliability incentives under uncertain contingency models
open: Determine how reserve prices and security charges should change when the set, dependence, and probabilities of credible failures are themselves uncertain.
status: Contingency-based pricing frameworks provide explicit treatment of selected security states. They do not eliminate uncertainty about which states should be represented.
why: Pricing errors can reward nominal reliability while overlooking common-mode risk.
key_works: Ribeiro et al. (2025), causation-based energy, reserve, and transmission pricing, arXiv:2505.24159.

title: Atomic identity of LeTID-active defect complexes
open: Identify the defect complexes and charge-state transitions responsible for light- and elevated-temperature-induced degradation across relevant silicon materials and processing histories.
status: Hydrogen-based explanations reproduce important observations, but reproducing degradation kinetics is not equivalent to uniquely identifying the microscopic defect.
why: Enables targeted prevention instead of process recipes that work only empirically.
key_works: D. Chen et al. (2020), *Hydrogen-induced degradation: Explaining the mechanism behind light- and elevated temperature-induced degradation in n- and p-type silicon*, DOI:10.1016/j.solmat.2019.110353.

title: Processing-dependent reservoirs of degradation-active hydrogen
open: Predict how firing, cooling, dielectric deposition, and subsequent illumination distribute hydrogen among beneficial passivation sites and latent degradation reservoirs.
status: Studies show strong dependence on thermal processing and cooling history. The unresolved target is a predictive inventory model, not merely another empirically improved anneal.
why: Allows passivation and long-term stability to be optimized together.
key_works: D. Chen et al. (2020), DOI:10.1016/j.solmat.2019.110353; *Understanding the impact of the cooling ramp of the fast-firing process on light- and elevated-temperature-induced degradation* (2023), DOI:10.1016/j.solmat.2023.112462.

title: Coupled ultraviolet and potential-induced degradation
open: Predict module behavior when ultraviolet exposure and electrical potential drive interacting degradation or recovery processes rather than independent monotonic damage.
status: The 2025 IEA PVPS assessment reports that ultraviolet exposure can interact with potential-induced degradation, including mitigation in some TOPCon conditions.
why: Sequential qualification tests may miss failure pathways created by simultaneous stresses.
key_works: M. Köntges et al. (2025), *Degradation and Failure Modes in New Photovoltaic Cell and Module Technologies*, IEA-PVPS T13-30:2025.

title: Thin-glass module fracture under combined loads
open: Predict fracture probabilities from manufacturing flaws, mounting, thermal gradients, wind, and residual stress in large thin-glass modules.
status: The 2025 IEA PVPS assessment identifies breakage concerns in newer module constructions. Passing an individual load test does not establish lifetime reliability under combined histories.
why: Material savings must not cause disproportionate field replacement.
key_works: Köntges et al. (2025), IEA-PVPS T13-30:2025.

title: Arsenic activation without compensating defects in CdTe
open: Predict and control the competition between electrically useful group-V dopants and compensating defect configurations during growth, treatment, and operation.
status: In-situ group-V doping enabled CdTe efficiencies above 20% in 2019. That achievement does not establish unrestricted control over activation and compensation.
why: Higher useful carrier concentration can improve voltage without relying on uncontrolled impurity migration.
key_works: W. K. Metzger et al. (2019), *Exceeding 20% efficiency with in situ group V doping in polycrystalline CdTe solar cells*, DOI:10.1038/s41560-019-0446-7; T. Ablekim et al. (2017), *Self-compensation in arsenic doping of CdTe*.

title: Defect-configuration completeness in CdTe alloy modeling
open: Determine whether computational searches have missed low-energy charged defects or complexes, and quantify the effect of those omissions on predicted carrier concentrations and recombination.
status: DeFecT-FF uses active learning and high-throughput calculations to explore broad Cd/Zn–Te/Se/S defect spaces. Exhaustive coverage and uncertainty under new chemistry remain unresolved.
why: An accurate model of an incomplete defect list can still make incorrect device predictions.
key_works: M. H. Rahman, M. Biswas, and A. Mannodi-Kanakkithodi (2026), *DeFecT-FF: a machine learning force field framework for high throughput defect modeling in CdTe-based solar cells*, arXiv:2510.23514; DOI:10.1039/D6CP00170J.

title: Narrow-bandgap CIGS voltage retention
open: Reduce recombination and voltage deficits as CIGS composition is tuned toward narrow bandgaps suitable for tandem bottom cells, without losing collection or stability.
status: Zhang et al. reported enhanced-voltage narrow-bandgap devices in 2024. A successful composition and process do not close the broader bandgap-dependent defect problem.
why: Makes tandem architectures less dependent on sacrificing voltage in their bottom absorber.
key_works: J. Zhang et al. (2024), *Highly efficient narrow bandgap Cu(In,Ga)Se₂ solar cells with enhanced open circuit voltage for tandem application*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-54818-6.

title: Predictive CIGS metastability under changing illumination
open: Predict reversible and irreversible changes in CIGS performance under illumination, bias, temperature, and storage histories using identifiable defect-state dynamics.
status: Metastability effects are documented, including under low-intensity and low-temperature conditions. Standard-test stabilization does not necessarily reproduce actual operating history.
why: Improves performance forecasts for applications outside ordinary terrestrial test conditions.
key_works: H. Afshari et al. (2020), *The role of metastability and concentration on the performance of CIGS solar cells under low intensity low temperature conditions*.

title: Net-efficiency-positive singlet-fission silicon interfaces
open: Couple singlet-fission absorbers to silicon while preserving silicon passivation and obtaining more collected electrical energy than the interface’s optical and recombination penalties consume.
status: Singlet-fission enhancement has experimental foundations; a 2026 design study analyzes routes beyond 30% silicon-cell efficiency. A complete, durable device at that level remains the target.
why: Converts molecular excitation multiplication into useful photovoltaic output.
key_works: S. McNab et al. (2026), *Silicon Solar Cell Design for >30% Efficiency via Singlet Fission*, arXiv:2609.10979; M. V. Klymenko et al. (2023), arXiv:2310.15736.

title: Disentangling collective quantum effects in singlet fission
open: Determine when collective excitonic correlations materially change triplet generation and extraction in disordered, finite-temperature photovoltaic films.
status: A 2026 theoretical study analyzes collective excitonic entanglement. Demonstrating a device-relevant advantage requires discriminating those effects from ordinary morphology and kinetic changes.
why: Identifies whether sophisticated quantum descriptions supply actionable design variables.
key_works: L. I. Payne and D. A. Mazziotti (2026), *Collective Excitonic Entanglement in Singlet Fission*, arXiv:2608.13785.

title: Energy-selective contacts without excessive heat leakage
open: Build hot-carrier contacts that extract a narrow energy range while retaining useful electrical conductance and suppressing unwanted heat exchange.
status: Nonideal-contact analysis quantifies how heat flow undermines hot-carrier conversion. Perfectly selective model contacts do not establish a realizable device.
why: Slow cooling in an absorber is insufficient without a compatible extraction mechanism.
key_works: A. S. Sharma et al. (2023), *Heat Flow through Nonideal Contacts in Hot-Carrier Solar Cells*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevApplied.20.034001.

title: Hot-carrier cooling suppression at operating illumination
open: Retain a useful nonequilibrium carrier population at realistic solar photon flux, rather than only at excitation densities that create unusually favorable phonon bottlenecks.
status: Slow hot-carrier cooling is observed in halide perovskites. Its dependence on excitation density and extraction conditions remains central to device relevance.
why: Prevents ultrafast spectroscopy under intense excitation from being mistaken for solar operating performance.
key_works: M. Li et al. (2019), *Slow Hot-Carrier Cooling in Halide Perovskites: Prospects for Hot-Carrier Solar Cells*, DOI:10.1002/adma.201802486.

title: Perovskite reverse-bias survival under realistic shading
open: Prevent irreversible local damage when module-level shading forces perovskite cells into reverse bias, including repeated events and realistic protection circuitry.
status: Improved reverse-bias stability has been demonstrated through contact and electrode design. That does not establish lifetime survival across module fault and shading histories.
why: Ordinary outdoor shading must not become a destructive electrochemical event.
key_works: F. Jiang et al. (2024), *Improved reverse bias stability in p–i–n perovskite solar cells with optimized hole transport materials and less reactive electrodes*, Nature Energy 9, 1275–1284.

title: Tandem-level fault protection with unequal subcell breakdown
open: Coordinate subcell design, interconnection, and bypass protection when tandem components have different reverse-bias characteristics and degradation pathways.
status: Reverse-bias resilience of monolithic perovskite–silicon tandems has been studied. A robust cell is not automatically protected once connected into a larger module.
why: Avoids transferring electrical stress from one subcell or module region to another.
key_works: *Reverse-bias resilience of monolithic perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells* (2023), Joule; Jiang et al. (2024), reverse-bias-stability study.

title: Preventing incongruent melting in salt-hydrate storage
open: Preserve composition and recoverable latent heat when melting produces phases of different composition that segregate under gravity and repeated cycling.
status: Additives, encapsulation, and composite approaches mitigate segregation, but their effectiveness depends on material, geometry, and operating history.
why: Initial calorimetric capacity is useless if the storage medium separates during use.
key_works: J. Sun et al. (2025), *Review of salt hydrates materials in phase change heat storage and thermochemical heat storage: mechanism, optimization method and application*, DOI:10.1016/j.applthermaleng.2025.127291.

title: Reliable on-demand crystallization of supercooled heat stores
open: Trigger crystallization when requested while avoiding spontaneous discharge during storage, with reliability maintained over many cycles and changing impurity populations.
status: Supercooling and nucleation control are well studied, but simultaneously obtaining long retention and dependable triggering remains material- and device-specific.
why: Makes stored latent heat dispatchable rather than dependent on accidental nucleation.
key_works: Sun et al. (2025), salt-hydrate storage review, DOI:10.1016/j.applthermaleng.2025.127291.

title: Predictive selection of deliquescent hydration additives
open: Predict when a hygroscopic additive accelerates useful hydration and when it instead creates transport barriers, unwanted liquid phases, or slower conversion.
status: A systematic selection framework appeared in 2023; subsequent work shows that extremely hygroscopic salts do not necessarily accelerate hydration.
why: Hygroscopicity alone is an inadequate screening criterion.
key_works: N. Mazur et al. (2023), *A systematic deliquescent additive selection approach for enhancement of reaction kinetics of thermochemical heat storage materials*, DOI:10.1016/j.solmat.2023.112588; M. Cotti et al. (2025), hydration-kinetics study.

title: Hydration kinetics across pellet and reactor scales
open: Predict reaction-front speed and usable power when pellet swelling, pore blockage, heat release, and vapor supply interact across an entire packed bed.
status: Salt-hydrate kinetics and heat release have been measured for many candidates. Small-sample rates do not directly determine packed-bed discharge power.
why: Distinguishes a high-capacity material from a store that can deliver heat quickly enough.
key_works: H. U. Rammelberg, T. Schmidt, and W. Ruck (2012), *Hydration and dehydration of salt hydrates and hydroxides for thermal energy storage—kinetics and energy release*, Energy Procedia 30, 362–369.

title: Minimizing useful-temperature loss from hydration hysteresis
open: Reduce the temperature and humidity hysteresis required to charge and discharge a thermochemical store while retaining practical reaction rates and stable cycling.
status: Materials screening increasingly accounts for reaction hysteresis. A thermodynamically large storage capacity does not guarantee heat recovery at the temperature required by the user.
why: Preserves the quality, not only the quantity, of stored heat.
key_works: Mazur et al. (2023), deliquescent-additive selection study, DOI:10.1016/j.solmat.2023.112588; Rammelberg et al. (2012), hydration-kinetics study.

title: Useful room-temperature hydrodynamic heat transport
open: Demonstrate that phonon-hydrodynamic transport provides a net thermal-management advantage in a packaged structure with contacts, defects, finite dimensions, and realistic heat sources.
status: Room-temperature second sound in isotopically pure graphite was reported in 2026. Its observation is solved context; useful device-level heat removal is a different target.
why: Converts a striking transport regime into an engineering benefit.
key_works: Z. Xie et al. (2026), *Room-temperature second sound in isotopically pure graphite*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70807-3.

title: Distinguishing second sound from ballistic thermal signatures
open: Establish measurement criteria that separate collective hydrodynamic heat waves from ballistic propagation and mixed transport when several phonon populations coexist.
status: Experiments have observed second sound in graphite from elevated cryogenic temperatures through room temperature. Interpretation in new geometries still requires discrimination among transport regimes.
why: Prevents assigning a collective mechanism to an ambiguous transient signal.
key_works: S. Huberman et al. (2019), *Observation of second sound in graphite at temperatures above 100 K*, DOI:10.1126/science.aav3548; Xie et al. (2026), DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70807-3.

title: Thermal-rectification bounds with useful forward conductance
open: Derive achievable tradeoffs between rectification, forward heat throughput, temperature range, geometry, and permitted material properties for specified thermal-diode classes.
status: Bounds and optimal designs exist under restricted conductivity laws. Maximizing a rectification ratio alone can favor a device that carries almost no useful heat.
why: Defines performance targets that cannot be gamed by suppressing both directions.
key_works: Y. Yang et al. (2018), *Optimal thermal rectification of heterojunctions under Fourier law*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevE.98.042131.

title: Separating intrinsic rectification from contact effects
open: Measure and model how temperature-dependent contact resistance, pressure, and surface topography contribute to apparent thermal rectification.
status: A 2025 numerical study shows that contact resistance can either suppress or enhance rectification. Device behavior cannot always be attributed to bulk material asymmetry.
why: Enables reproducible comparisons and prevents misleading mechanism claims.
key_works: K. Vozel and A. Kitanovski (2025), *Numerical study of macroscopic thermal diodes: Influence of interface topography and contact resistance*, DOI:10.1016/j.isci.2025.113724.

title: Broad-temperature thermal-diode material discovery
open: Identify affordable material pairs and interfaces that maintain useful rectification and conductance over a broad operating interval rather than near one narrow transition temperature.
status: Vozel and Kitanovski identify systematic material-pair exploration as a remaining need. Temperature-dependent conductivity and contact effects make the optimum application-specific.
why: Broad operating windows are essential for variable industrial and building conditions.
key_works: Vozel and Kitanovski (2025), macroscopic thermal-diode study, DOI:10.1016/j.isci.2025.113724.

title: Persistent permeability beyond conventional brittle behavior
open: Create connected flow paths in superhot rock and demonstrate that they remain useful under the temperatures, stresses, and chemical conditions expected during prolonged circulation.
status: Watanabe et al. demonstrated cloud-fracture networks in high-temperature experiments. Initial permeability creation does not establish long-duration reservoir performance.
why: Determines whether accessible superhot rock can become a usable heat exchanger.
key_works: N. Watanabe et al. (2019), *Cloud-fracture networks as a means of accessing superhot geothermal energy*, PMCID:PMC6353971.

title: Shut-in-induced closure of superhot flow paths
open: Predict how permeability changes when pressure and temperature evolve during shutdown, restart, and emergency cooling, including irreversible closure.
status: Experiments on pressurized flow through deforming artificial rock show that permeability depends on brittle and ductile deformation history.
why: A reservoir that works continuously may fail to restart after an interruption.
key_works: S. Sulieman et al. (2023), *Investigating the Permeability Evolution of Artificial Rock During Ductile and Brittle Deformation Under Pressurized Flow*, arXiv:2309.02231.

title: Constitutive laws linking subcritical cracking to reservoir lifetime
open: Couple time-dependent crack growth, creep, stress redistribution, and chemical alteration into a constitutive model that predicts geothermal permeability over operational timescales.
status: New long-timescale brittle constitutive models incorporate subcritical crack growth. Connecting them to evolving hydraulic properties and geothermal chemistry remains additional work.
why: Bridges short laboratory tests and decades of subsurface operation.
key_works: L. Petit et al. (2024), *A brittle constitutive law for long-term tectonic modeling based on sub-critical crack growth*, arXiv:2401.15784.

title: Supercritical-fluid phase transitions in geothermal flow networks
open: Predict where changing pressure, temperature, and salinity cause phase separation, density contrasts, or precipitation that reorganize circulation near superhot resources.
status: Hydrological models describe superhot and supercritical resource behavior, but coupled phase transitions and heterogeneous permeability complicate site-specific predictions.
why: A high-temperature resource can lose injectivity or useful circulation through fluid-property changes.
key_works: S. Scott (2018), *The hydrology of ‘superhot’ and ‘supercritical’ geothermal resources in magma-driven geothermal systems*, GRC Transactions 42, 2476–2492.

title: Cooling-induced fracture connectivity without uncontrolled damage
open: Predict when thermal contraction produces a useful connected network rather than isolated microcracks, unstable larger fractures, or damaging near-well fragmentation.
status: Compressive-shear phase-field models and high-temperature fracture experiments provide components of the theory. Reliable prediction of connectivity under cooling remains a coupled problem.
why: Thermal stimulation must increase useful heat exchange rather than merely damage rock.
key_works: S. Zhou, X. Zhuang, and T. Rabczuk (2023), *Phase field modeling of brittle compressive-shear fractures in rock-like materials: A new driving force and a hybrid formulation*, arXiv:2308.05748.

title: Scaling laboratory permeability laws to superhot reservoirs
open: Determine which dimensionless groups and measurements permit laboratory fracture and permeability results to be extrapolated to heterogeneous field-scale reservoirs.
status: Cloud-fracture and pressurized-deformation experiments establish important mechanisms, but differ substantially in specimen size, boundary conditions, and duration from operating reservoirs.
why: Prevents unvalidated scale extrapolation from dominating project forecasts.
key_works: Watanabe et al. (2019), *Cloud-fracture networks*; Sulieman et al. (2023), arXiv:2309.02231.

title: Fully coupled OTEC cold-water-pipe dynamics
open: Predict large cold-water-pipe behavior under platform motion, currents, internal flow, buoyancy, and nonlinear structural deformation together.
status: Nonlinear bending analyses provide useful component evidence. They do not establish the complete coupled response of a large offshore installation.
why: The intake pipe is a major reliability and deployment constraint for ocean thermal energy conversion.
key_works: P. W. Adie et al. (2023), *Non-linear assessment of cold water pipe (CWP) on the ocean thermal energy conversion (OTEC) installation under bending load*, DOI:10.1016/j.prostr.2023.07.005.

title: Vortex-induced fatigue qualification for OTEC intakes
open: Predict fatigue damage over realistic current profiles, changing tension, marine growth, and intermittent extreme events, then validate mitigation at relevant scale.
status: Vortex-excited oscillation has been recognized as an OTEC pipe-design problem since at least 1981. Modern materials and geometries require renewed lifetime validation.
why: Avoids a design that survives a static load but fails through accumulated oscillatory damage.
key_works: O. M. Griffin (1981), *OTEC cold water pipe design for problems caused by vortex-excited oscillations*; Adie et al. (2023), DOI:10.1016/j.prostr.2023.07.005.

title: Pressure-retarded-osmosis membranes at net-positive system power
open: Maintain sufficient water permeability and mechanical integrity at useful pressure while controlling salt leakage, concentration polarization, and pumping requirements.
status: Power-station models and optimization exist. Membrane power density alone does not establish positive net output from a complete installation.
why: Separates impressive membrane measurements from an energy-producing system.
key_works: F. Di Michele et al. (2019), *Modeling, simulation and optimization of a pressure retarded osmosis power station*, DOI:10.1016/j.amc.2019.01.046.

title: Adaptive operation of osmotic power with variable real feeds
open: Optimize pressure, flow, staging, and cleaning when salinity, temperature, suspended material, and membrane condition vary over time.
status: Station-level models optimize specified conditions. Real-feed variability and progressive fouling require dynamic decisions rather than a fixed design-point optimum.
why: Determines whether salinity-gradient resources remain useful outside controlled feed conditions.
key_works: Di Michele et al. (2019), pressure-retarded-osmosis power-station study, DOI:10.1016/j.amc.2019.01.046.

title: Multivalent-ion selectivity without resistance penalties in reverse electrodialysis
open: Control multivalent-ion transport without increasing membrane resistance enough to erase the recovered voltage or concentration-gradient benefit.
status: Moreno et al. showed that suppressing undesirable magnesium transport can fail to improve power because resistance rises. More selective is not automatically better.
why: Natural seawater and river water are not sodium-chloride-only solutions.
key_works: J. Moreno et al. (2018), *Mitigation of the effects of multivalent ion transport in reverse electrodialysis*, DOI:10.1016/j.memsci.2017.12.069.

title: Reverse-electrodialysis performance after pretreatment and maintenance
open: Demonstrate persistent net electricity production after feed pretreatment, circulation, cleaning, electrode-system losses, and membrane replacement are included.
status: Pilot-scale studies using selective membranes establish useful operating evidence. Stack gross power is not the complete lifecycle energy balance.
why: Prevents parasitic water handling from consuming the energy being harvested.
key_works: S. Mehdizadeh et al. (2021), *Power Generation Performance of a Pilot-Scale Reverse Electrodialysis Using Monovalent Selective Ion-Exchange Membranes*, PMID:33401447.

title: Silver transport through apparently intact TRISO silicon carbide
open: Resolve which pathways allow silver release through nominally intact silicon-carbide coatings, including grain boundaries, defects, pores, and trapping.
status: The issue has persisted for decades. A 2026 model combines grain-boundary simulations and uncertainty analysis, but requires additional trapping physics to reconcile transport estimates.
why: Determines whether coating integrity alone is sufficient evidence for fission-product retention.
key_works: H. J. MacLean (2004), *Silver transport in CVD silicon carbide*; M. AbdulHameed et al. (2026), *Modeling of silver transport in cubic SiC: Integrating molecular dynamics, bounds averaging, and uncertainty quantification*, arXiv:2508.14325; DOI:10.1103/1nt8-9hly.

title: Microstructure-transferable TRISO release coefficients
open: Predict fission-product release for a new silicon-carbide coating from its measured grain-boundary and pore statistics, without refitting an empirical diffusivity to that coating’s release data.
status: The 2026 silver-transport study explicitly treats microstructural averaging and uncertainty. Transfer across manufacturing routes and irradiation histories remains a stronger test.
why: Enables manufacturing qualification based on relevant microstructure rather than nominal material identity.
key_works: AbdulHameed et al. (2026), silver-transport modeling, arXiv:2508.14325; DOI:10.1103/1nt8-9hly.

title: Freeze-plug actuation across the full reactor operating history
open: Demonstrate reliable passive thawing and drainage following loss of active cooling across low-power, startup, shutdown, and nominal-power thermal histories.
status: A 2019 molten-salt fast-reactor study shows that thawing behavior depends strongly on geometry and available heating. Passive actuation cannot be assumed from material melting temperature alone.
why: The shutdown mechanism must function when the preceding operating state is unfavorable.
key_works: M. Tiberga et al. (2019), *Preliminary investigation on the melting behavior of a freeze-valve for the Molten Salt Fast Reactor*.

title: Diagnosing partial thawing and degradation of freeze valves
open: Detect changes in plug shape, thermal contact, contamination, and partial melting that could cause failure to open or unintended opening.
status: Freeze-valve designs and historical operating experience have been reviewed, but dependable state estimation and lifetime assurance remain design-specific.
why: A nominally passive component can still develop hidden failure states.
key_works: B. M. Chisholm et al. (2020), *A unique molten salt reactor feature—The freeze valve system: Design, operating experience, and reliability* — exact punctuation **(verify)**, PII:S0029549320302971.

title: Validity limits of point kinetics in circulating-fuel reactors
open: Determine when reduced point-kinetics models fail because delayed-neutron precursors move through spatially varying neutron importance, temperature, and flow fields.
status: A 2025 comparison of MSRE modeling approaches examines spatial dynamics and point kinetics. Validation on selected low-power and pump transients does not establish all full-power scenarios.
why: Fuel motion changes the relationship between local reactions and total reactor response.
key_works: P. Pfahl et al. (2025), *Comparison of spatial dynamics and point kinetics approaches in multiphysics modeling of the molten salt reactor experiment*, DOI:10.3389/fnuen.2025.1617048.

title: Delayed-neutron-data uncertainty in flowing-fuel stability
open: Quantify how uncertainty in precursor yields and decay data combines with uncertain transport and thermal feedback to alter stability margins.
status: A 2025 study directly examines delayed-neutron-data uncertainty in molten-salt dynamics. Joint uncertainty with evolving flow and composition remains a further requirement.
why: Small nuclear-data uncertainties can be amplified by circulation and feedback.
key_works: T. Abuqudaira, P. Tsvetkov, and P. Sabharwall (2025), *Effect of Delayed Neutron Data Uncertainty on Molten Salt Reactor Dynamics Simulations*, Transactions of the American Nuclear Society 133, 792–795.

title: Air-ingress transition to buoyancy-driven graphite oxidation
open: Predict when an initial gas-exchange process becomes sustained natural circulation and how that transition changes oxidation, heat release, and structural damage.
status: Air-ingress research has a long history, and a 2025 review examines remaining thermal-hydraulic questions following depressurized loss of forced cooling.
why: The rate-limiting process can change during the event, invalidating a single-regime calculation.
key_works: M. Scheel, P. Sabharwall, R. Schultz, and G. Blois (2025), *A review on the state of thermal hydraulics research on air ingress scenarios in High-Temperature Gas-cooled Reactors following a D-LOFC*.

title: Microstructure-resolved steam oxidation of nuclear graphite
open: Predict oxidation and strength loss from graphite grade, pore structure, temperature, steam concentration, and prior irradiation rather than relying only on bulk mass-loss correlations.
status: Grade-specific steam-oxidation measurements exist, including studies of IG-110. Transferring those measurements across microstructures and exposure histories remains unresolved.
why: Equal mass loss can produce different mechanical consequences depending on where oxidation occurs.
key_works: Y. J. Cho et al. (2020), *Water vapor oxidation behaviors of nuclear graphite IG-110…* — full subtitle **(verify)**, Carbon, PII:S0008622320303237.

title: Transferable irradiation-creep laws for nuclear graphite
open: Predict irradiation creep for a new graphite grade from its microstructure, temperature, stress history, and neutron exposure, with uncertainty bounds that remain valid outside the calibration dataset.
status: Wang and colleagues used machine learning to investigate graphite irradiation-creep coefficients in 2025. Predicting coefficients within available measurements does not establish transfer to new grades or coupled, changing irradiation conditions.
why: Reliable creep predictions are needed to estimate component distortion and stress redistribution without conducting a complete lifetime experiment for every material.
key_works: Y. Wang et al. (2025), *Insights into irradiation creep coefficient in nuclear graphite from machine learning*, DOI:10.1016/j.net.2025.103559.

title: Quantitative transfer from ion irradiation to neutron damage
open: Determine which combinations of ion species, energy, dose rate, temperature, and specimen geometry reproduce particular neutron-induced graphite changes, and identify observables for which no reliable correspondence exists.
status: Wilczopolska and colleagues compared structural and microstructural damage produced under different irradiation conditions in 2025. Similar accumulated damage metrics do not automatically imply equivalent defect populations or bulk mechanical behavior.
why: Validated surrogates could accelerate qualification; invalid ones can produce confidently wrong lifetime estimates.
key_works: M. Wilczopolska et al. (2025), *Evolution of radiation-induced damage in nuclear graphite—a comparative structural and microstructural study*, arXiv:2502.11851.

title: Selective carbon-14 removal from heterogeneous irradiated graphite
open: Remove a useful fraction of carbon-14 while minimizing destruction of the graphite matrix, secondary waste, energy consumption, and uncontrolled radioactive gas release across different irradiation histories.
status: Limited oxidation has been demonstrated as a way to remove surface-associated carbon-14. That result does not establish equivalent selectivity when the isotope occupies different chemical environments or is distributed deeper within components.
why: Selective treatment could reduce disposal burdens without converting the entire graphite inventory into a more difficult waste stream.
key_works: T. E. Smith, S. McCrory, and M. L. Dunzik-Gougar (2013), *Limited oxidation of irradiated graphite waste to remove surface carbon-14*, Nuclear Engineering and Technology 45, 211–218.

title: Maintaining the protective oxygen window in lead coolants
open: Control oxygen activity throughout a lead or lead–bismuth circuit so protective surface layers persist without excessive oxide precipitation, including cold regions, transients, and changing material inventories.
status: Oxygen management is an established corrosion-control strategy. The 2022 materials assessment documents competing dissolution, oxidation, and precipitation processes that prevent one nominal bulk oxygen concentration from guaranteeing protection everywhere.
why: A chemistry setting that protects one component can foul or damage another.
key_works: X. Gong et al. (2022), *Environmental degradation of structural materials in liquid lead- and lead-bismuth eutectic-cooled reactors*, DOI:10.1016/j.pmatsci.2022.100920.

title: Predictive liquid-metal embrittlement under reactor loading
open: Predict when liquid-metal exposure changes crack initiation and propagation under realistic combinations of stress, temperature, irradiation, surface condition, and oxygen chemistry.
status: Susceptibility is experimentally established for particular material–environment combinations, but corrosion resistance and resistance to liquid-metal embrittlement are not interchangeable properties.
why: A component can exhibit acceptable mass loss while remaining vulnerable to mechanically driven failure.
key_works: Gong et al. (2022), liquid-lead materials assessment, DOI:10.1016/j.pmatsci.2022.100920.

title: Quantified defect detection by under-sodium ultrasound
open: Establish probability-of-detection and localization-error bounds for relevant defects and obstructions under sodium, including temperature gradients, wetting changes, bubbles, and inaccessible geometries.
status: Patel and Kumar reported scaled-core experimental work on under-sodium ultrasonic imaging in 2025. Successful imaging in a controlled model does not establish detection reliability throughout an operating reactor.
why: Inspection quality must be expressed in terms of missed defects and false indications, not only recognizable images.
key_works: D. Patel and A. Kumar (2025), *Experimental simulation of under sodium ultrasonic imaging in a sodium cooled fast breeder reactor using a scaled down model of the core*, DOI:10.1016/j.anucene.2024.111127.

title: Early sodium–water leak detection with defensible alarm thresholds
open: Infer small developing leaks from hydrogen measurements while separating sensor drift, background chemistry, transport delay, and ordinary operating changes.
status: Yamamoto and colleagues investigated hydrogen behavior relevant to sodium–water reaction detection in 2024. Translating that behavior into a reliable early-warning system requires an identifiable leak-to-sensor model.
why: Detection must be early enough to limit damage without making operation impractical through frequent false alarms.
key_works: T. Yamamoto et al. (2024), *Fundamental evaluation of hydrogen behavior in sodium for sodium-water reaction detection of sodium-cooled fast reactor*, DOI:10.1016/j.net.2023.10.043.

title: Artifact-free tests of hydrogen-assisted bearing failure
open: Design experiments that distinguish hydrogen’s causal contribution to bearing damage from damage introduced by the hydrogen-charging procedure itself.
status: López-Uruñuela and colleagues compared electrochemical and immersion hydrogen uptake in bearing steel in 2025. Charging-induced changes to the material can confound attempts to attribute later failures solely to hydrogen.
why: Mechanistically misleading accelerated tests can favor ineffective countermeasures for premature drivetrain failures.
key_works: F. J. López-Uruñuela et al. (2025), *A study on the influence of electrochemical and immersion hydrogen uptake methodologies on 100Cr6 bearing steel integrity*, DOI:10.1016/j.ijhydene.2025.02.273.

title: Long-horizon effects of intermittent water ingress in pitch bearings
open: Predict damage from repeated episodes of water contamination, drying, lubricant replacement, and changing loads, rather than treating water content as a fixed test parameter.
status: Short-term pitch-bearing water-ingress experiments were reported in 2024. They do not determine whether apparently recoverable contamination leaves latent damage that accelerates later wear.
why: Maintenance decisions depend on whether removing contaminated grease restores the bearing or merely hides continuing damage.
key_works: M. Stammler et al. (2024), pitch-bearing water-ingress study, Lubricants 12, 310, DOI:10.3390/lubricants12090310.

title: Grease replenishment under small-amplitude oscillation
open: Predict when pitch-bearing motion replenishes lubricated contacts and when it repeatedly removes lubricant without sufficient redistribution, including changing oscillation amplitudes and dwell times.
status: Pitch-bearing endurance research recognizes that oscillatory operation differs fundamentally from continuously rotating bearing tests. A transferable lubrication-and-wear model remains more useful than a single successful test schedule.
why: Control actions that reduce aerodynamic loads can inadvertently create unfavorable lubrication conditions.
key_works: M. Stammler (2020), *Endurance test strategies for pitch bearings of wind turbines*, doctoral dissertation, DOI:10.15488/10080.

title: Field-calibrated fatigue prediction for large roller pitch bearings
open: Validate rolling-contact fatigue calculations against sufficiently representative service histories, including ring deformation, manufacturing variation, lubrication, and nonuniform roller loading.
status: Menck, Schleich, and Stammler developed detailed fatigue calculations for a three-row roller pitch bearing in 2025. Numerical stress resolution does not itself validate accumulated lifetime damage.
why: Accurate contact mechanics must translate into credible failure probabilities and replacement intervals.
key_works: O. Menck, F. Schleich, and M. Stammler (2025), *Rolling contact fatigue calculation of a three-row roller pitch bearing in a wind turbine*, DOI:10.5194/wes-10-2771-2025.

title: Adhesive fatigue under nonproportional multiaxial blade loading
open: Predict crack initiation and growth in blade adhesive joints when normal and shear stresses change direction and phase, without reducing the history to an inadequately justified scalar equivalent stress.
status: Balzani and Noever Castelos quantified nonproportional stress histories in trailing-edge joints in 2025. Characterizing those histories does not supply a universally validated fatigue law.
why: Laboratory tests using proportional loads can miss damaging features of real blade operation.
key_works: C. Balzani and P. Noever Castelos (2025), *Non-proportionality analysis of multi-axial fatigue stress histories in trailing edge adhesive joints of wind turbine rotor blades*, DOI:10.5194/wes-10-1249-2025.

title: Coupled buckling and adhesive-fatigue progression
open: Predict the feedback between local blade deformation, adhesive cracking, stiffness loss, and subsequent changes in the loading path.
status: Detailed joint-stress analysis exposes loading complexity, but treating geometry and stiffness as unchanged throughout fatigue can miss the feedback produced by growing damage.
why: A joint may transition from slow deterioration to rapid failure as structural load redistribution accelerates cracking.
key_works: Balzani and Noever Castelos (2025), blade-joint stress-history analysis, DOI:10.5194/wes-10-1249-2025.

title: Wind-farm blockage in convective boundary layers
open: Predict farm-scale upstream flow modification across convective boundary-layer depths and surface-heating conditions, including the transition between weak and consequential blockage.
status: Ndindayino and Meyers investigated blockage in convective conditions in a 2026 preprint. Their large-eddy simulations provide evidence against assuming that convection automatically removes farm-scale blockage.
why: Plant yield and spacing estimates can be biased before turbine wakes are even considered.
key_works: O. Ndindayino and J. Meyers (2026), *Wind farm blockage in convective boundary layers*, DOI:10.5194/wes-2026-49; associated dataset DOI:10.48804/QWUDVE.

title: Error-controlled reduced models for shared-mooring wind farms
open: Build reduced models that preserve important platform and line-load responses as farm size, sea state, and mooring configuration change, with explicit error bounds.
status: Rajasree, Sauder, and Bachynski-Polic demonstrated modal reductions in 2026 and found important differences between dynamic and quasistatic line models in studied configurations.
why: Shared moorings cannot be optimized efficiently if accurate analysis always requires the full coupled model.
key_works: V. R. N. Rajasree, T. Sauder, and E. E. Bachynski-Polic (2026), *Dynamic behaviour of floating wind farms with shared mooring in waves—Part II: Modal description and mooring line model fidelity*, DOI:10.1016/j.oceaneng.2026.124911.

title: Failure containment in shared-mooring arrays
open: Determine whether a failed line or anchor can trigger unacceptable excursions, overloads, or collisions elsewhere in a shared-mooring farm, and design configurations that contain such failures.
status: Mooring-failure response has been simulated for individual floating turbines, while shared-mooring dynamics introduces additional pathways for load redistribution.
why: Savings from shared infrastructure must not introduce a disproportionate common-mode failure risk.
key_works: Y. Ren et al. (2020), *Dynamic Responses of Spar Type Floating Offshore Wind Turbine Under Mooring Failure Conditions*; Rajasree et al. (2026), DOI:10.1016/j.oceaneng.2026.124911.

title: Field benchmarks for floating-wind mooring damage detection
open: Assemble labeled, reusable field data that distinguish genuine line damage from changing sea state, operating condition, sensor drift, and model error.
status: A 2026 replication dataset supplies simulated chain- and synthetic-line damage cases. It is useful for controlled comparisons but is not a substitute for independent field validation.
why: A detector trained on a simulator may learn the simulator’s damage assumptions rather than real precursors.
key_works: C. Sakaris et al. (2026), *Replication Data for: Damage detection in chain and synthetic mooring lines of Floating Offshore Wind Turbines*, DOI:10.18710/LSVFOL.

title: Optimal tow-to-port versus offshore repair decisions
open: Choose repair location and timing while accounting for failure progression, disconnection risks, vessel availability, port constraints, weather uncertainty, and lost production.
status: The 2022 floating-wind marine-operations assessment identifies major differences between available maintenance strategies. A universally cheapest strategy cannot be inferred from repair cost alone.
why: Maintenance architecture can determine whether floating projects achieve useful availability.
key_works: R. C. Ramachandran et al. (2022), *Floating wind turbines: marine operations challenges and opportunities*, DOI:10.5194/wes-7-903-2022.

title: Forecast-aware certification of offshore maintenance windows
open: Select operational windows using probabilistic forecasts that correctly account for forecast error, correlated waves and wind, operation duration, and the consequences of interruption.
status: Offshore workability analyses exist, but a window predicted from deterministic weather thresholds is not a guarantee that a multistage operation can finish safely.
why: Reduces both avoidable waiting and unsafe commitment to incomplete weather windows.
key_works: Ramachandran et al. (2022), marine-operations assessment, DOI:10.5194/wes-7-903-2022.

title: Net-positive, durable blade anti-icing
open: Operate anti-icing systems so recovered annual generation exceeds heating, control, maintenance, and aerodynamic penalties across realistic icing events.
status: Positive-temperature-coefficient heating materials were investigated for wind-blade anti-icing in 2025. Preventing ice on a test surface does not establish a favorable whole-turbine lifetime energy balance.
why: An effective heater can still be an ineffective energy intervention.
key_works: M. Wang, Y. Zhao, and Y. Lin (2025), *Anti-icing performance of electric heating for wind turbine blades based on the positive temperature coefficient material*, DOI:10.1016/j.coldregions.2025.104749.

title: Long-lived inert anodes for molten-oxide iron electrolysis
open: Sustain oxygen evolution at useful current density while limiting anode dissolution, contamination of iron, protective-layer failure, and replacement cost.
status: Allanore, Yin, and Sadoway demonstrated an important oxygen-evolving anode material in 2013. A promising composition does not establish industrial campaign life across variable oxide feeds.
why: Consumable or rapidly degrading anodes can erase the intended emissions and cost advantages.
key_works: A. Allanore, L. Yin, and D. R. Sadoway (2013), *A new anode material for oxygen evolution in molten oxide electrolysis*, DOI:10.1038/nature12134.

title: Lower-temperature iron electrolysis with competitive current efficiency
open: Improve useful iron yield per unit electricity in lower-temperature molten electrolytes while maintaining product purity, electrolyte stability, and practical throughput.
status: Choi and colleagues demonstrated iron electrolysis in sodium-borate melts at 1,000 °C, reporting 54.7% current efficiency under their studied conditions. This establishes feasibility, not an optimized industrial process.
why: Reduced temperature is valuable only if electrical losses and processing requirements do not outweigh it.
key_works: H. G. Choi et al. (2021), *Electrolysis of iron with oxygen gas evolution from molten sodium borate electrolytes*, DOI:10.1080/03019233.2020.1861837.

title: Water escape during hydrogen reduction of iron oxides
open: Predict and control how newly formed water leaves evolving oxide–metal microstructures, including closed pores and channels that change as reduction proceeds.
status: El-Zoka and colleagues directly investigated the fate of water during hydrogen-based reduction in 2023. Bulk reaction-rate models can miss local water accumulation and its effect on continued reduction.
why: Gas supply alone does not determine reduction speed when the reaction product becomes trapped.
key_works: A. A. El-Zoka et al. (2023), *The Fate of Water in Hydrogen-Based Iron Oxide Reduction*, DOI:10.1002/advs.202300626; arXiv:2301.06391.

title: Copper removal from heterogeneous steel scrap without excessive iron loss
open: Remove residual copper across realistic scrap mixtures while preserving iron recovery and avoiding reagent, separation, or energy demands that exceed the benefits.
status: Daehn, Serrenho, and Allwood compared removal routes in 2019. Their analysis distinguishes technically possible separation from the most efficient complete process.
why: Copper accumulation limits the grades that can be produced from increasingly recycled steel.
key_works: K. E. Daehn, A. C. Serrenho, and J. M. Allwood (2019), *Finding the most efficient way to remove residual copper from steel scrap*, DOI:10.1007/s11663-019-01537-9.

title: Low-loss vacuum refining of copper-contaminated steel
open: Obtain useful copper evaporation rates while minimizing radiative heat loss, vacuum-system consumption, iron evaporation, and recontamination.
status: Vacuum distillation is among the investigated routes for residual-copper removal, but theoretical separation energy omits potentially decisive equipment and heat-loss penalties.
why: A favorable thermodynamic separation does not necessarily produce an efficient steelmaking operation.
key_works: Daehn, Serrenho, and Allwood (2019), copper-removal process comparison, DOI:10.1007/s11663-019-01537-9.

title: Impurity-tolerant electrochemical cement precursors
open: Produce consistent cement-forming precursors electrochemically from variable mineral feeds while controlling electrode fouling, unwanted precipitation, impurity partitioning, and gas purity.
status: Ellis and colleagues demonstrated an electrolyzer-based carbonate-decomposition route that produces useful streams. Extending controlled-feed chemistry to industrial raw materials remains an integration challenge.
why: Feed purification must not become a hidden cost or energy burden larger than the process improvement.
key_works: L. D. Ellis et al. (2020), *Toward electrochemical synthesis of cement—An electrolyzer-based process for decarbonating CaCO₃ while producing useful gas streams*, DOI:10.1073/pnas.1821673116.

title: Joint quality control for steel and electrically recycled cement
open: Co-produce acceptable steel and cementitious material despite changing scrap and recovered-paste compositions, without optimizing one product at the expense of the other.
status: Dunant and colleagues demonstrated electric recycling of Portland cement at scale in 2024. The result establishes a promising integrated route, not unrestricted compatibility among all input streams and product specifications.
why: Industrial adoption requires both co-products to remain useful and saleable.
key_works: C. F. Dunant et al. (2024), *Electric recycling of Portland cement at scale*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07338-8.

title: Low-energy separation of cement paste from demolished concrete
open: Recover sufficiently clean cement paste from mixed demolition material without excessive grinding, heating, aggregate damage, or loss of fine material.
status: Electrically recycled cement depends on appropriate recovered feed. Demonstration of the downstream recycling chemistry does not remove the upstream separation problem.
why: Collection and separation can govern the practical scale of an otherwise effective recycling route.
key_works: Dunant et al. (2024), cement-recycling study, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07338-8.

title: A transferable sulfate optimum for limestone–calcined-clay cement
open: Select sulfate content that jointly supports hydration, workability, setting, strength development, and durability across varying clay mineralogy and processing.
status: The 2024 comparison of sulfate-optimization techniques identifies limitations in existing approaches. An optimum derived from one measurement need not optimize all performance criteria.
why: Small formulation changes can affect both manufacturability and long-term performance.
key_works: M. R. Cardoso da Silva et al. (2024), *Exploring sulfate optimization techniques in Limestone Calcined Clay Cements (LC3): limitations and insights*, DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2023.107375.

title: Long-term qualification of low-grade clays and calcined wastes
open: Determine which low-grade clays and waste-derived calcined materials yield durable binders across exposure conditions, rather than qualifying them only through short-term strength.
status: Krishna and colleagues evaluated additional material candidates in a 2026 Australian case study. Early-age performance does not establish resistance to decades of chemical and physical exposure.
why: Broader feedstock availability is useful only when local materials produce dependable infrastructure.
key_works: R. S. Krishna et al. (2026), *Can calcined waste materials and low-grade clays be part of the limestone calcined clay cement binder system? An Australian case study*.

title: Transient hot-spot control in electrically heated reformers
open: Coordinate electrical heating and reaction rates during startup, shutdown, and feed changes so local temperatures remain controlled without sacrificing useful ramping speed.
status: Compact electrified reforming was demonstrated in 2019, followed by dedicated transient analysis. Rapid electrical response does not imply equally rapid or uniform chemical and thermal response.
why: Uncontrolled local temperatures can damage catalysts or structures even when average reactor temperature appears acceptable.
key_works: S. T. Wismann et al. (2019), *Electrified methane reforming: A compact approach to greener industrial hydrogen production*, DOI:10.1126/science.aaw8775; Wismann et al. (2021), *Electrified methane reforming: Elucidating transient phenomena*.

title: Impurity-tolerant electrified biogas reforming
open: Maintain catalyst and electrically heated structure performance when biogas composition and trace contaminants change, including realistic cleanup failures and recovery procedures.
status: From and colleagues reported a pilot study of electrified biogas reforming in 2024. Pilot operation does not establish lifetime tolerance across the range of commercial biogas sources.
why: Excessive feed purification can negate the value of processing a variable renewable gas.
key_works: T. N. From et al. (2024), *Electrified steam methane reforming of biogas for sustainable syngas manufacturing and next-generation of plant design: A pilot plant study*, Chemical Engineering Journal, PII:S1385894723059363.

title: Olefin-separation membranes under industrial mixtures
open: Retain selectivity and permeance at relevant pressures and compositions when feeds contain multiple hydrocarbons, water, trace contaminants, and condensable species.
status: The 2021 industrial assessment emphasizes that attractive membrane properties must be evaluated under process-relevant conditions rather than idealized single-gas tests.
why: Olefin–paraffin separation is energy-intensive, but membrane performance can deteriorate under the very mixtures it must separate.
key_works: A. Roy et al. (2021), *Membranes for olefin–paraffin separation: An industrial perspective*, DOI:10.1073/pnas.2022194118.

title: Lifetime-stable olefin membrane modules
open: Prevent aging, plasticization, defect growth, and seal degradation from erasing useful separation performance over long operating campaigns.
status: Material-level selectivity is insufficient to establish module lifetime; industrial deployment also depends on fabrication quality, operating history, and replacement requirements.
why: A membrane that initially saves energy may become uneconomical through rapid replacement or declining purity.
key_works: Roy et al. (2021), industrial membrane assessment, DOI:10.1073/pnas.2022194118.

title: Reproducible sub-ångström control in carbon molecular sieves
open: Manufacture carbon adsorbents or membranes with consistently useful ultramicropore distributions while retaining throughput, mechanical strength, and resistance to fouling.
status: Du and colleagues demonstrated precise light-olefin/paraffin separation associated with sub-5-ångström micropores in 2023. Laboratory structural control does not establish economical production of large uniform modules.
why: Tiny pore-distribution changes can determine whether molecular sieving works at all.
key_works: S. Du et al. (2023), *Probing sub-5 Ångstrom micropores in carbon for precise light olefin/paraffin separation*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-023-36890-6.

title: Electrified-cracker scheduling without hidden process damage
open: Coordinate variable electricity, storage, and cracking operations while explicitly accounting for product quality, fouling, catalyst or tube life, and restart penalties.
status: A 2025 study optimizes microgrid scheduling for cleaner olefins production. Optimization results depend on how faithfully the model represents allowable process flexibility.
why: Electricity-price savings are not beneficial if they accelerate maintenance or reduce product yield.
key_works: S. Ghasemi Naraghi et al. (2025), *Decarbonization of Steam Cracking for Clean Olefins Production: Optimal Microgrid Scheduling*, arXiv:2510.25880.

title: Recoverable geological hydrogen versus modeled subsurface stock
open: Estimate the fraction of modeled geological hydrogen that can be located, reached, produced at useful rates, and recovered without unacceptable losses or energy consumption.
status: Ellis and Gelman modeled global geological hydrogen resources in 2024. An estimated subsurface stock is not a reserve estimate or evidence of commercially recoverable flow.
why: Resource-scale claims are otherwise easily mistaken for deliverable energy supply.
key_works: G. S. Ellis and S. E. Gelman (2024), *Model predictions of global geologic hydrogen resources*, DOI:10.1126/sciadv.ado0955.

title: Distinguishing hydrogen replenishment from depletion of stored gas
open: Infer whether sustained well output is supplied by ongoing generation, redistribution from surrounding pores, or depletion of a finite accumulation.
status: Geological-hydrogen research explicitly separates generation, migration, accumulation, and consumption. Production over a limited interval does not uniquely identify the rate of replenishment.
why: Sustainable production forecasts require knowing which source actually supports the flow.
key_works: Sandia National Laboratories, *Geologic Hydrogen* research program; Ellis and Gelman (2024), DOI:10.1126/sciadv.ado0955.

title: Identifiable source-and-sink models for natural hydrogen
open: Combine gas composition, isotopes, tracers, microbiology, and pressure histories to distinguish competing generation mechanisms and quantify subsurface hydrogen consumption.
status: Current research investigates multiple sources and sinks, but several combinations can produce similar observed gas concentrations.
why: Exploration and production strategies depend on whether a low measured concentration reflects weak generation, rapid consumption, or poor accumulation.
key_works: Sandia National Laboratories, *Geologic Hydrogen*; S. E. Gelman, T. E. Hearon, and G. S. Ellis (2025), *Prospectivity mapping for geologic hydrogen*, USGS Professional Paper 1900.

title: Sustained reactivity during stimulated serpentinization
open: Maintain useful hydrogen generation as reactive surfaces become altered, flow paths change, and reaction products restrict access to fresh minerals.
status: A 2026 Oman field-study abstract reports injection and recovery experiments in serpentinized peridotite. Recovering hydrogen-rich fluids does not by itself demonstrate persistent stimulation of commercially useful generation.
why: An initial hydrogen pulse may not indicate a durable production process.
key_works: J. Shannon et al. (2026), *Stimulating Hydrogen Generation in Serpentinised Peridotite: Field-Scale Injection Experiments in Oman*, EGU conference abstract, DOI:10.5194/egusphere-egu26-3339.

title: Field mass balances for net-new stimulated hydrogen
open: Demonstrate how much hydrogen was newly generated by an intervention, rather than released from pre-existing accumulations, and account for unrecovered gas and competing reactions.
status: Field injection and pumpback studies provide valuable observations, but causal attribution requires baseline inventories, tracers, and complete enough balances to distinguish mobilization from generation.
why: Production claims and stimulation economics depend on the additional hydrogen actually caused by the intervention.
key_works: Shannon et al. (2026), Oman field experiments, DOI:10.5194/egusphere-egu26-3339.

title: Joint optimization of hydrogen generation and carbon mineralization
open: Determine when conditions favorable for carbonation support or suppress hydrogen-producing reactions, including competition for reactive surfaces and effects on permeability.
status: A 2026 reaction-profile study explicitly examines serpentinization versus carbonation. Treating hydrogen production and carbon storage as automatically synergistic ignores their chemical and hydraulic interactions.
why: Proposed dual-purpose projects require a demonstrated joint benefit, not two favorable processes considered independently.
key_works: Q. Xiong et al. (2026), *Serpentinization versus carbonation: geochemical and thermodynamic constraints from an ophiolitic reaction profile*, DOI:10.5194/egusphere-egu26-3638.

title: Ortho–para conversion integrated with hydrogen liquefaction
open: Place and operate conversion stages so their released heat is removed efficiently across changing flow rates, while limiting pressure drop and incomplete conversion.
status: Cryogenic ortho–para conversion is established technology, and CSIRO has investigated its simulation and testing within liquefaction processes. The open target is improved integrated performance, not discovery of the conversion.
why: Poorly managed conversion heat can increase refrigeration demand or later boil-off.
key_works: CSIRO (2022), *Simulation and testing of cryogenic ortho-para conversion in hydrogen liquefaction processes*.

title: Lifetime qualification of cryogenic hydrogen-conversion catalysts
open: Predict catalyst performance after contamination, thermal cycling, mechanical attrition, and long exposure, including safe detection of declining conversion.
status: Conversion behavior can be measured in controlled cryogenic systems; translating fresh-catalyst results into maintainable industrial operation requires additional lifetime evidence.
why: Catalyst deterioration can shift an initially acceptable liquefaction process into excess heat release downstream.
key_works: CSIRO (2022), cryogenic ortho–para conversion research.

title: Continuous carbon removal from liquid-metal methane pyrolysis
open: Remove changing carbon morphologies without blocking gas flow, entraining excessive liquid metal, destabilizing the reactor, or imposing costly downstream purification.
status: Continuous reactor concepts and operation have been investigated; the 2024 technical assessment identifies carbon handling among the coupled challenges of liquid-metal bubble columns.
why: A reactor that converts methane but cannot continuously discharge its solid product is not a complete production process.
key_works: C. Hofberger et al. (2024), *Technical Aspects of Natural Gas Pyrolysis in Liquid Metal Bubble Column Reactors*, DOI:10.1002/ente.202400183.

title: Thermal versus nonthermal mechanisms in induction-assisted pyrolysis
open: Determine whether reported activity enhancement comes from electromagnetic effects beyond heating or from unresolved local temperature distributions, and quantify any independently reproducible nonthermal contribution.
status: Ngo and colleagues reported induction-heated carbon-catalyst results in 2026 while discussing uncertainty about local heating and field effects.
why: The distinction governs reactor scale-up, temperature measurement, and whether a claimed catalytic advantage can be reproduced.
key_works: Ngo et al. (2026), *Breaking Methane without Metals: Induction-Heated Carbon Catalyst at Low-Temperature Process*, DOI:10.1002/aesr.202500503.

title: Closed material cycles for magnesium-assisted methane activation
open: Recover and reuse magnesium-containing catalytic phases while accounting for vapor losses, oxidation, carbon contamination, and the energy needed to restore their active state.
status: Vapor and molten magnesium-based methane-activation pathways were studied in 2025. High activity does not establish a low-consumption catalyst cycle.
why: A nominal catalyst must not become an expensive or energy-intensive sacrificial reagent.
key_works: J. Srivastava et al. (2025), *Vapor and Molten Mg-Based Catalysts for Methane Activation*, DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c05697.

title: Shaped covalent-organic-framework contactors without lost performance
open: Convert high-performing capture powders into mechanically stable, low-pressure-drop structures while preserving accessible capacity, adsorption kinetics, and efficient heat transfer.
status: Zhou and colleagues demonstrated open-air capture with COF-999 in 2024. Powder performance does not determine the energy and throughput of a packaged contactor.
why: Fans, heating, structural supports, and diffusion distances can dominate the complete capture system.
key_works: Z. Zhou et al. (2024), *Carbon dioxide capture from open air using covalent organic frameworks*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08080-x.

title: Ten-thousand-cycle qualification of COF air-capture sorbents
open: Meet a **proposed target of 10,000 representative capture–regeneration cycles with less than 10% loss of usable capacity**, including real-air contaminants and mechanically shaped material.
status: COF-999 research includes approximately one hundred-cycle laboratory durability evidence. That is encouraging but does not establish the proposed longer-life target.
why: Sorbent replacement can determine both capture cost and lifecycle environmental burden.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2024), COF-999 capture study, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08080-x.

title: Joint optimization of water and carbon-dioxide adsorption
